articles.title: Madness of Nuclear War
articles.author: Lawrence S. Wittner
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Is there a connection between mental illness and nuclear weapons? The behavior of Donald Trump?whose mental stability has long been questioned by psychologists and other mental health professionals?has called attention to this issue. In March and early April of this year, he threatened to launch massive military strikes against Iranian energy and nuclear infrastructure, proclaiming on April 5 : “There will be nothing like it!!! Open the Fuckin’ Strait, you crazy bastards, or you’ll be living in Hell – JUST WATCH!” On April 7, he warned : “A whole civilization will die tonight, never to be brought back again. I don’t want that to happen, but it probably will.” Addressing the UN General Assembly on September 22, Trump threatened to “annihilate” Iran, saying that he could “drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future . . . generations.” Assessing Trump’s UN diatribe, the Union of Concerned Scientists declared that it “constitutes an implied threat to use overwhelming nuclear force against Iran and the Iranian people”?a “nuclear genocide.” Related: National Security Has Failed. Is International Security the Answer? Observers were aghast . U.S. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said Trump sounded like “a madman,” while Senator Bernie Sanders called Trump’s remarks “the ravings of a dangerous and mentally unstable person.” Referring to Trump’s rant on April 5, Senator Chris Murphy called it “absolute madness.” This May, 30 U.S. psychiatrists and other doctors specializing in mental health issued a statement declaring that Trump was mentally unfit to serve and warning that his ability to launch a nuclear weapons attack constituted a “danger” to the world. They noted, among other things, his “severely impaired judgment and impulse control,” “significant loss of self-control,” and “grandiose and delusional beliefs, including assertions of infallibility.” Russia’s Vladimir Putin has also been diagnosed , repeatedly , as suffering from mental disorders. Certainly his behavior in connection with nuclear weapons has been remarkably menacing. According to a Voice of America report , Putin publicly issued 27 nuclear threats between February 2022 and December 2024. He talked of “preventive disarming nuclear strikes,” promised four times to nuke Germany if it delivered Leopard battle tanks to Ukraine, ordered Russian nuclear forces to simulate a nuclear attack on Ukraine, and announced that Russia’s strategic nuclear forces “are in a state of full combat readiness for a guaranteed use.” When, in a televised interview, the CEO of a state media giant asked Putin if Russia was ready for nuclear war, he responded blithely: “Weapons exist to be used.” Nor are other leaders of nuclear-armed nations, such as North Korea’s Kim Jong Un, Israel’s Benjamim Netanyahu, and India’s Narendra Modi, paragons of mental health and military restraint. Actually, the alarming connection between mental instability and nuclear weapons has long been evident. In March 1946, less than a year after the atomic bombings of Japan, an article appeared in The Saturday Review of Literature with the title: “Gentlemen: You are Mad!” The author, Lewis Mumford?a well-known American historian, sociologist, and philosopher of technology?explained: “The madmen are planning the end of the world. What they call continued progress in atomic warfare means universal extermination.” In June 1957, when a group of prominent Americans met at New York City’s Overseas Press Club to consider what should be done about the issue of nuclear weapons testing, they adopted a similar stance. “The normal drive for survival has been put out of action by present propaganda,” remarked Erich Fromm, an eminent psychoanalyst. “We must . . . try to bring the voice of sanity to the people.” Establishing a new organization, they called it the National Committee for a Sane Nuclear Policy. SANE, as the new group was usually dubbed, began with the goal of halting nuclear testing but soon broadened that to securing nuclear disarmament. Related: Trump's War on the International Criminal Court Threatens Global Justice As nuclear disarmament organizations emerged around the world in the late 1950s and early 1960s, they frequently depicted nuclear war as madness . SANE named its newsletter Sane World , while Britain’s Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament and the Canadian Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament both called their newsletters Sanity . Even government officials agreed on occasion that nuclear war was insane. In November 1957, as Nikita Khrushchev recalled , China’s Mao Zedong gave a speech that lauded nuclear war at a meeting of Communist party leaders from around the world. “We may lose more than three hundred million people,” Mao reportedly said. But “so what. War is war.” Finding Mao’s remarks “deeply disturbing,” Khrushchev came away convinced that his ally was a lunatic and eventually cut off Soviet assistance to China’s nuclear weapons program. U.S. President John F. Kennedy also took up the nuclear insanity theme. Speaking before the UN General Assembly in September 1961, he warned that “every man, woman and child lives under a nuclear sword of Damocles, hanging by the slenderest of threads, capable of being cut at any moment by accident or miscalculation or by madness.” Two years later, in a major address on nuclear weapons and war, he cautioned that nuclear war could be launched “by a madman.” Although, in the following decades, a combination of popular pressure and government response managed to curb the nuclear arms race and avert a nuclear holocaust, the world seems once again in the grip of government officials all too eager to prepare for and launch a nuclear war. Related: How Trump’s Labor Policies Are Cutting Worker Pay This enormous nuclear danger magnifies the importance of the first review conference for the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons , scheduled to occur at the United Nations from November 30 to December 4. Although signed by a majority of the world’s nations, this landmark treaty has been rejected thus far by the nuclear powers. But if they signed and implemented the treaty, it would effectively ban nuclear weapons and their immense danger to human survival. Will humanity seize the opportunity offered by the treaty? Or are we all too mad to comprehend the fact that, as long as nuclear weapons exist, we live on the brink of nuclear annihilation? PeaceVoice

articles.title: On Clear Tasks and Meetings
articles.author: Rochester Red Star: News from Rochester DSA
articles.content: by Jean Allen This essay is written in support of my convention resolution, For A Collectively Printed & Distributed Red Star . In it, I am motioning that we budget $3,600 for a printer and future printing costs through the year, and I understand that seems to be a lot. It will be compared to other front-facing work we have, other important committees, and people will ask why we should devote so much energy, time, and money to our publication? This resolution should be seen more as a partial solution to a problem brought up by our ambitions. In our first long term planning retreat, we agreed to aim for a membership of 1000 within the next five years. Some comrades have brought up fears that are, broadly, about the quality of that new mass membership. What if they are liberals, or reactionaries? What if these members do not aid in the capacity of the chapter, and instead stay as ‘paper members’? I want to cast the first problem wholly away. I do not have the politics I had when I joined DSA. In fact, the politics I have now did not exist when I joined DSA, but instead emerged from the interaction of hundreds of people with practical organizing . That is the experience of so many comrades in our organization, and I see no reason that it will cease being the case in the future. What we should worry about, more than what the new members call themselves the moment they join, is: what will we give them to do ? When I joined ROC DSA, the organization was two years old and we were just figuring ourselves out. What kind of work would we do, what were the boundaries of our politics, why are we even doing anything we did? There was a degree of pressure then, in 2017-2020, for us to become similar to the other left wing organizations around us at the time. Groups like Metro Justice dwarfed us, and had a clear eyed focus on basebuilding, mobilizing, and lobbying towards the end of getting radical legislation passed. Other organizations were even more focused on lobbying. A criticism I had of this approach is that lobbying focuses us on very specific people – it requires getting enough members who have free time, specialized skills, and the drive to get in a bus at 5AM on a weekday to go to Albany and pressure our electeds to little effect. I believed that we needed, instead, something that could produce a mass politics. But I have a self-criticism. Far too often, the answer I and our chapter had to a new member asking “what do I do about the growth of fascism in the US?” is to say “clear a weekday, you’re going to be in a meeting deciding what we’ll do!”. Our meetings have gotten better, and as a whole we are far better at meeting discipline than we were in 2023 (when, during the primary season, we had more meetings than days in the month). But those criticisms I had of lobbying – that it requires people with free time, specialized skills, and the drive to keep going without clear wins – all apply to meetings-as-praxis. They also require specialized skills, they all require drive, and in fact they require more of our free time. Now, I am not saying that meetings are bad, and I am very much not saying that we should stop deliberating. But if meetings are for the purpose of making decisions about the work we are doing, far too often the leadership work of filtering day to day activities into something people can meaningfully make a decision on, and making decisions into tasks that are assigned and then followed up on, is left to the meeting, and so meetings become multiple people deciding on the logistics of something that one person should be figuring out, rather than thinking about the broader direction we are going in. If we are going to be an organization of thousands of members, that has hundreds of active members, then we will need to give those members something they can meaningfully do. For the most active, that may look like meetings and making dozens upon dozens of decisions about the tactics and logistics of the chapter. Ideally, general meetings would be a place where all the decisions are filtered to a place where membership can meaningfully choose strategic directions. But for many, many members, their engagement will look like something smaller. Anyone who’s been to a labor training will have seen this graphic: The ‘core’ for us is leadership, the hyper-engaged, people who know a bunch that’s going on and who have a high level of time commitment to the chapter. Outside of that is activists, people who are engaged but perhaps not consistent, who maybe don’t have a fully formed idea of what they want to do with the chapter. Further outside are supporters (who maybe show up to a meeting every so often) and the disengaged (who are, at best, paper members). Something that was brought up to me the first time I was shown this has stuck with me since: that the best way to get a member to move deeper into the bullseye is to get them to feel they are representing the organization in some way. They get the ‘big sibling’ educational effect, where older siblings who are forced to teach their younger siblings end up reinforcing their grasp of the material by expressing the lesson in their own words. So a disengaged member, who is expressing socialist ideas to their friends, is finding their own way to articulate them. A supporter who tables for us ends up having dozens of conversations where they’re speaking on behalf of all of us, and it gives them a better sense of what they want from this organization and how they can help us. This could be an argument for any clearly defined, front facing set of tasks, and I want to be clear I support us engaging in all of them more. City Vitality has done very well for its clear outward facing task. But this resolution centers Red Star, and gives whatever priority campaign we have reserved column space, for a reason. For the development of our chapter’s rich inner life, we are not yet, as a chapter, in the habit of explaining our political perspective externally. We are good at slogans, we are good at developing conversations internal to the chapter, we are getting better at developing campaigns towards the political ends we’ve decided on, but when it comes to arguing our beliefs in depth, that is a skill that many members have, but which we do not have as an organization. When our leaders in the Steering Committee attended a pretty hostile interview on WXXI the other month, there were several times they seemed stumped. I do not think this is a failing of these comrades, it is a failing of a chapter culture which hasn’t developed the habit of putting out clear socialist analysis. This is understandable as we’ve worked to build, from the ground up, a socialist organization in this city. But just like meeting centricity, it is not fitted to a truly mass politics. We need to get better at creating smaller, outward-facing, manageable tasks if we want to become a truly mass organization. We can do that without giving up the rich internal life we have built for ourselves in ROC DSA. City Vitality’s outreach walks and External Organizings’ tablings are two examples, but we need more, easily manageable tasks, for the organization to thrive. And for us to win, in our long term goal of the working class governing society, we need to get far more comfortable with articulating ourselves to it. People are excited, desperate, to do something in this moment. We need something to say, and something to do. The post On Clear Tasks and Meetings first appeared on Rochester Red Star .

articles.title: We Can Abolish the Electoral College in 2027
articles.author: Will Bloom
articles.content: With Democrats taking trifectas in state governments they have not held for a long time, DSA can campaign to get rid of a deeply undemocratic feature of our political life: the Electoral College. The newly blue state governments mean we can functionally end the Electoral College through the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact (NPVIC) . At a moment where a Democratic Congress is likely to be more focused on oversight than on legislating, DSA could accomplish something meaningful and powerful that actually inches our country toward democracy. What Is the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact? The Electoral College is a wholly undemocratic way to elect the most powerful individuals in the world. Candidates for President and Vice President are not elected by the people but by “electors” selected by states. Notably, the method of selection of electors is left up to the states themselves. Most use winner-take-all; the total state popular vote elects one slate of electors pledged to the winning candidate. Voters for the losing side essentially do not count. Only Maine and Nebraska choose electors on a congressional-district-by-congressional-district basis (which is still undemocratic), with the statewide vote determining their final two electors. The undemocratic impact of the Electoral College has been felt since the founding, but in recent decades its effects have been pronounced, helping Republicans secure control of the executive branch. Four presidents have been elected by the Electoral College while losing the popular vote, two of them in this century. George W. Bush lost the popular vote in 2000 but took the White House. Hillary Clinton defeated Donald Trump by nearly 3 million votes in 2016; without the Electoral College, Trump would have been rendered a historical curiosity. Fortunately, there’s a vehicle we can use to scrap the Electoral College, in effect: the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact. Proposed in 2006 by a former elector, the NPVIC is a binding agreement among the states that sign on. Legislatures can pass a bill directing their state to join the Compact, and the governor signs it. States that sign on agree that, once states representing an absolute majority of electors have joined, they will all change the way they choose their electors. At their ceremonial post-election voting in their state capitals, they will ratify a slate of electors pledged to the candidate who won the largest popular vote across all 50 states and D.C. In this way, while the Electoral College would formally remain in place, its distorting effects would be eliminated, and the winner of the popular vote would become the President. The Opportunity As of now, states representing 222 electoral votes have ratified the Compact (Maine, Vermont, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Connecticut, New York, New Jersey, Delaware, Maryland, Virginia, Illinois, Minnesota, Colorado, New Mexico, Washington, Oregon, California, and the District of Columbia). To take effect, the Compact needs to be ratified by states with a total of 270 electoral votes. Efforts to pass the Compact in more states have historically run into opposition from Republicans. But as of this election, there are now Democratic trifectas in five new states that have not yet ratified the Compact: Pennsylvania, Michigan, Wisconsin, Nevada, and (likely at time of writing) Arizona. Those five states have 61 electoral votes between them, more than enough to trigger the Compact. Those states include some of DSA’s strongest chapters, as well as several DSA-endorsed state legislators. Over the next nine to twelve months, DSA should campaign nationally to get these states to pass the Compact. We would be organizing around a broadly popular demand. Our chapters in key states could pressure governors and legislative leaders. Our SIOs in those legislatures could lead on passage. At the same time, chapters could develop political education that connects this particular demand with DSA’s Workers Deserve More demands for real democracy. Functionally ending the Electoral College would be a massive structural change in our political system towards democracy, and something we can win even while Donald Trump remains President. If DSA takes a lead on this fight and wins, we can show working class people energized by the midterm repudiation of Trump, who are likely to be disappointed by meek Democratic Party leaders, that real victories can be accomplished — if we win through popular agitation and organizing. The campaign will also help us deepen our power and organization in five states that are vitally important in electoral and other work, especially with an eye on 2028. We are already starting to see some in the progressive movement encourage the new trifectas to take up the Compact. DSA, though, has some advantages in taking the lead that those non-socialist forces lack. Our newly elected Pennsylvania Congressman Chris Rabb led on passing the Compact as a state legislator in Harrisburg , introducing the legislation and conducting hearings on it last year. DSA state Representative Dylan Wegela cosponsored legislation in Michigan to sign onto the Compact earlier this year. DSA legislators in Pennsylvania, Michigan, and Wisconsin are all well-positioned to push the necessary legislation. Most important, our thousands of member-organizers mean that DSA can coordinate a national campaign with specific local targets. We have a rare opportunity to notch an early, major win in this new political moment. It will require us to act quickly before other issues begin to feel more pressing. By eliminating the Electoral College as a barrier to democracy, we can strengthen DSA and show that workers truly deserve more. The post We Can Abolish the Electoral College in 2027 appeared first on The Call .

articles.title: South Africa’s ANC Is Collapsing. The Far Right Is Rising.
articles.author: Zwelinzima Vavi
articles.content: While the global left celebrates the recent successes of the Workers’ Party in Brazil and the Democratic Socialists of America in the United States, the African National Congress (ANC) has suffered a historic collapse in South Africa’s November 4 local government elections. After three decades of mass unemployment, deepening inequality, corruption, and economic policies that have failed the working class, the former liberation movement is losing its political authority. The principal beneficiaries of the ANC’s electoral rout are parties of the Right, including an increasingly powerful far right that has built its project around aggressive and often violent xenophobia. With more than 70 percent of votes counted, the ANC’s national share of the vote fell to around 32 percent. The ANC is not expected to retain an outright majority in any major city, and the center-right Democratic Alliance (DA), historically the principal party of the white liberal establishment, is making substantial gains and is projected to become the largest party in most of South Africa’s big cities. Former President Jacob Zuma’s Zulu nationalist uMkhonto weSizwe Party (MKP) is on track to be the largest party in Durban. The far-right ActionSA has made a strong showing in Johannesburg and Pretoria and is likely to be the second-largest party in Pretoria, with the ANC in third place. The central question is not only why the ANC has lost so much support. It is why the suffering and anger of the working class have failed to produce a powerful democratic socialist alternative, and why the Right has been so successful in presenting itself as the answer to a crisis created by the existing economic and political order. The ANC’s Historic Failure The defeat of apartheid was an extraordinary achievement. We won universal suffrage, democratic institutions, constitutional rights, and legal protections for workers. Those victories were won through generations of sacrifice and collective struggle, and they must be defended. But political apartheid was defeated while the economic structures inherited from apartheid remained largely intact. The liberation movement historically brought together different classes and social groups united against racial oppression. That unity was indispensable to apartheid’s defeat. But national identity does not abolish class contradictions. Instead of using democracy to transform the ownership and control of the economy in the interests of the majority, the ANC increasingly became an instrument through which a new elite could enter and benefit from the existing economic order. The ownership and control of the commanding heights of the economy were never fundamentally transformed. Land ownership remained extraordinarily unequal. The former Bantustans, created as reservoirs of cheap African labor, were never provided with the productive economic foundations needed to overcome their inherited poverty. Over time, the ANC came to treat the advancement of an emerging black capitalist class as evidence of economic transformation. A narrow layer of businesspeople accumulated wealth, in some cases extraordinary wealth, through access to political power, state contracts, and opportunities created by the Black Economic Empowerment policy, while the overwhelming majority remained excluded from meaningful economic power. The ANC’s adoption of neoliberal economic policies in the 1990s deepened this problem. The language of economic liberation gave way to investor confidence, competitiveness, and market reform. Brutal austerity, liberalization, and dependence on private investment displaced the redistributive ambitions of the liberation struggle. We were repeatedly told that economic growth would eventually deliver employment and redistribution. We were also told that redistribution must wait for economic growth and the development of the productive forces. But if redistribution had to wait while productive capacity developed, why did South Africa simultaneously deindustrialize? We have become what I have described as a “warehouse economy.” We export raw materials and insufficiently processed mineral wealth, allow other countries to manufacture finished products, then import those products for domestic consumption. We export jobs embedded in raw materials and import unemployment embedded in finished goods. Factories have closed while warehouses have remained open. South Africa continues to extract enormous mineral wealth without developing the productive industries capable of turning that wealth into decent employment on the scale required. It is a very painful fact that, after decades of mass unemployment and deindustrialization, the poor are now poorer and more numerous than under apartheid. In the second quarter of 2026, South Africa’s official unemployment rate stood at 33.6 percent. Including people who want work but have stopped actively searching, the rate was 43.8 percent. Among young people age fifteen to twenty-four who were in the labor force, unemployment reached 62.8 percent. This crisis has meant the destruction of hope for millions of people. It has also been accompanied by the weakening of the organized working class. Mass unemployment undermines bargaining power, makes workers afraid to exercise their rights, and encourages casualization and precarious employment. A worker who knows that thousands of unemployed people are desperate for a job is in a much weaker position to resist exploitation. The crisis has also fragmented the working class itself. Millions of people are unemployed, casually employed, working in the informal economy, or moving between different forms of insecure work. Traditional trade unions organize only a section of this wider class. The working class cannot be reduced to people fortunate enough to receive a regular pay slip. The unemployed, precarious workers, labor-broker workers, informal workers, women carrying the burden of unpaid care, and young people who have never had secure employment must all be part of the social movement capable of transforming South Africa. At the same time, the combination of austerity and extreme corruption has resulted in the decay of the state and the collapse of public services. Municipalities have become centers of patronage, political competition over tenders, and the accumulation of private wealth. Water systems collapse, roads deteriorate, sewage flows through communities, and public transport becomes increasingly unreliable. It has become normal for even middle-class areas to go for weeks or even months without water, while the poor live among stinking piles of uncollected refuse. The crisis is also visible in the ANC’s conception of the state. A developmental state cannot simply outsource development and then claim the credit. It requires public institutions with the capacity to plan, build, maintain infrastructure, and provide services directly. South Africa has developed a system in which government contracts out essential functions while state capacity deteriorates. The result is an expanding network of contractors, consultants, and intermediaries whose accumulation depends on public expenditure, while the institutions responsible for serving the people become weaker. The tragic reality is that the ANC’s neoliberal policies have not simply failed to resolve the economic crisis. They have also undermined the credibility of the very idea of democratic transformation, opening the door to right-wing demagoguery. Corruption and the Destruction of Political Authority Economic failure has been compounded by the degeneration of political leadership. The ANC once insisted that leadership required exceptional qualities: political understanding, integrity, discipline, courage, humility, service, and sacrifice. Its own document, “Through the Eye of the Needle,” expressed the idea that leadership should be earned through commitment to the people rather than acquired through personal ambition. Today the competition for leadership largely revolves around factions, access to resources, control of organizational structures, and the distribution of positions. Political office has become a route to private accumulation. This cannot be understood merely as a series of individual moral failures. It is connected to a political culture in which access to the state and public wealth becomes a route to private economic advancement. Where the public sector is treated as a source of tenders and contracts rather than an instrument for meeting social needs, the distinction between political leadership and business accumulation becomes blurred. The result is a profound loss of moral authority. When working people see leaders acquiring enormous wealth while unemployment rises, schools deteriorate, hospitals struggle, and the water supply fails, they inevitably begin to lose confidence in the institutions that claim to represent them. The ANC’s electoral collapse is therefore not mysterious. It is the political expression of a much deeper social, economic, and organizational failure. At the same time, trade unions have been divided, and some have become very corrupt, as corrupt as the ANC. The capacity of unions and community organizations to develop working-class leaders has weakened. Organizations have often concentrated on internal contests or debates between established political figures instead of building the democratic power of ordinary people. Political education, once central to the union movement, has declined. With the exception of Abahlali baseMjondolo, the two-hundred-thousand-strong movement of the urban poor, community organizations have lost much of their former strength, with many collapsing completely. The Right Advances A rapidly growing Right has been very successful in redirecting legitimate popular anger away from those responsible for generalized social suffering and toward African and Asian migrants. Fascist organisations such as Operation Dudula and March and March have built movements around violent hostility toward African migrants. In communities devastated by unemployment, crime, and failing services, they offer a simple explanation: foreigners are responsible for the crisis. Political parties have increasingly adopted the same language. Like many centrist parties elsewhere in the world, the ANC made a profound error of political judgment in indulging organized xenophobia rather than opposing it. The two parties that have surged forward in these elections, ActionSA and the MKP, have both actively supported the xenophobic street thuggery that forced up to 150,000 migrants, including refugees and other documented migrants, from the country in a matter of months. This right-wing mobilization, which includes fascist elements, does not only target migrants. It increasingly argues that South Africa has too many rights, that the Constitution should be changed to do away with some of these rights, and that strong leaders should be freed from democratic constraints. The result is a political paradox. South Africa faces one of the most severe crises of unemployment and inequality anywhere in the world, yet the electoral beneficiaries of popular anger are largely forces advocating policies that will deepen inequality as they redirect anger toward vulnerable minorities. Renewing the Left The Left is also in crisis. For decades, the South African Communist Party (SACP) presented itself as the socialist component of the ANC-led alliance. Yet it remained politically committed to governments that implemented austerity, privatization, and other neoliberal policies. Its leaders participated in those governments while continuing to speak in the language of socialism and working-class liberation. The contradiction between revolutionary language and participation in the administration of neoliberal capitalism became increasingly difficult to ignore. This contradiction has never been satisfactorily resolved. Earlier this year, the SACP proposed convening a “Conference of the Left,” inviting organizations including the ANC and Zuma’s MKP, which had been on the streets with the xenophobic mobs. How could a conference claim to unite the Left while including a governing party responsible for decades of neoliberal economic policy and a political formation associated with state capture, ethnic chauvinism, and xenophobia? The independent South African Federation of Trade Unions (SAFTU) considered the invitation carefully and decided not to participate. Other progressive organizations, such as Abahlali baseMjondolo, took similar positions. Working-class unity is indispensable, but it must be based on principles and a shared program. A Left that abandons its defining commitments in pursuit of alliances with corrupt or reactionary organizations will not resolve the present crisis. It will only deepen it. Rebuilding Independent Working-Class Power The answer cannot be to demand that workers and the poor continue supporting political organizations that have repeatedly failed them. Nor can we respond to the advance of the Right with moral denunciations while leaving the underlying conditions of life unchanged. South Africa needs a new working-class political project rooted in a credible program of economic transformation. But no program, however coherent, will succeed without organized social power. A genuine working-class political alternative must emerge from renewed organization, political education, democratic debate, and collective struggle. The principles of such a movement cannot be negotiable. It must be independent of employers and the capitalist state, committed to socialism and worker democracy, and resolutely opposed to racism, xenophobia, sexism, patriarchy, and ethnic chauvinism. It must be internationalist in its outlook and rooted in the everyday struggles of workers and poor communities. Rebuilding working-class power also requires reconnecting workplace struggles with those of communities. Water is a workers’ issue. Electricity is a workers’ issue. Public transport, housing, health care, education, gender-based violence, and the climate crisis are all workers’ issues. The struggles of an employed factory worker cannot be separated from those of an unemployed young person, a mother trying to feed her children, a shack dweller fighting for water, or a community resisting the destruction of its environment. The organizations capable of creating a new political alternative will have to emerge from these connected struggles. South Africa’s democratic transition was a great victory for popular movements across the world. The possibility that its political future could now be shaped increasingly by xenophobic and authoritarian forces should concern everyone committed to democracy, equality, and international solidarity. articles.title: A Childlike Devotion Runs Through Godzilla Minus Zero
articles.author: Eileen Jones
articles.content: There’s a familiar but always thrilling moment in Godzilla Minus Zero when Godzilla is fighting the newer, faster, entirely more visually glamorous monster King Ghidorah — an immense three-headed, golden-ray-shooting dragon that seems set on destroying the human race — and Godzilla is losing. In fact, it seems Godzilla is beaten and dying. But then Godzilla goes deep and dredges up the last of his prehistoric mojo and comes back to win the brutal kaiju battle. Godzilla the destroyer from the sea becomes Godzilla the hero and savior of the Japanese protagonists watching in wide-eyed terror. All the viewer’s childhood love of Godzilla, who lumbers around on big, squat feet like a crude, clumsy dinosaur based on some devoted but impractical kid’s drawing, surges to the fore. Writer-director-CGI effects master Takeshi Yamazaki seems highly motivated by such lingering childhood feelings. He cautions us in interviews, in a caringly paternal sort of way, to remember that though Godzilla fights King Ghidorah, it’s not because he sides with human beings: “He can’t become humanity’s friend.” Oh, we know . But many small children aren’t entirely on the side of humans either. Personally, I was all for the animals as a kid and relentlessly pretended to be an animal for years before the US educational system crushed it out of me. And most little children are united, at least for a few years, in a love of dinosaurs that borders on obsession. Though I’ve known a few kids who loved and identified with cars and trucks and industrial vehicles more than adult people. Yamazaki seems to understand all that. He says he opted to revive King Ghidorah and have him wreak havoc on Yamazaki’s own hometown of Matsumoto in the first scene of destruction in Godzilla Minus Zero , then fight the climactic epic battle with Godzilla because, fifty-five years ago, he was a seven-year-old kid in Matsumoto eagerly awaiting a revival screening of the Godzilla movie sequel Ghidorah, the Three-Headed Monster from 1964. The promotional flyer specifically promised, “King Ghidorah attacks Matsumoto!” But he was terribly disappointed when “the monster finally appeared [and] all he did was clip the roof tiles of the city’s castle before flying off.” Yamazaki said, “I was so frustrated, so heartbroken. . . . I held a grudge for years.” But ultimately, it’s heartwarming the way Yamazaki has been able to channel his childhood commitment and frustration into making the gorgeous and emotionally compelling Godzilla Minus One , released in 2023 and Godzilla Minus Zero , currently playing in theaters. It goes a long way toward explaining the immense critical and popular appeal of both. Yamazaki was stunned by the global success of the first film, which he claimed he never expected to get such a warm reception beyond Japan. Its embrace by mass audiences in the United States was especially surprising, since we’re notorious for refusing to see “foreign films” requiring us to read subtitles. But a grand exception is made in the case of Yamazaki’s Godzilla films. And Yamazaki isn’t conciliating American feelings either. Given the subject matter, it wouldn’t make any sense. In Godzilla Minus Zero , the characters representing the US military brass in post–World War II Japan are all sinister, arrogant conquerors clearly up to no good, always plotting ways to harness additional power and further subjugate the Japanese. Even the lowly GIs stationed in Tokyo are portrayed as a disturbing alien presence — jittery, full of directionless aggressivity, vaguely looking for trouble. One American soldier chews gum with a manic ferocity. The satirical portrayal of this platoon looks a lot like British filmmakers Michael Powell and Emeric Pressburger’s 1946 take on American GIs in A Matter of Life and Death , and Powell and Pressburger were being conciliatory to the United States in a “hands-across-the-pond” manner. Their GI Joes, killed near the end of World War II, arrive in heaven all hopped up on a similarly strange, angsty energy and immediately scramble over to a suddenly revealed vending machine stocked with Coca-Cola. Set in 1949, Godzilla Minus Zero has no humor of that kind. It’s a somber film entirely preoccupied with the relentless calamities besetting Japan: World War II, the US nuclear bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, living in postwar poverty and wreckage, the Godzilla attacks in Godzilla Minus One , and the King Ghidorah attacks in Godzilla Minus Zero . The character of Kanji Murakami (Min Tanaka), the elderly biologist who found the charred bodies of his family in the aftermath of the bombing of Hiroshima, miraculously comes through all the mayhem, exclaiming bitterly, “And again, I survive!” Min Tanaka plays the role of the biologist Kanji Murakami in Godzilla Minus Zero . (Toho Studios / Robot Communications) He joins forces to face the King Ghidorah threat with Kenji Noda (Hidetaka Yoshioka), director of the government’s Large-Scale Disaster Response Bureau, who has to put together the reluctant team that will fight this new monster. Former kamikaze pilot Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki), who flew the mission that apparently destroyed Godzilla in the previous film, is hoping — in vain — to avoid having to go up against King Ghidorah. Kōichi has married Noriko Ōishi (Minami Hamabe), a survivor of a previous Godzilla attacks, and together they’ve adopted war orphan Akiko (Sae Nagatani). The investment in their new family gives them a great stake in escaping any further life-threatening calamities. Director Yamazaki particularly wanted a woman represented among the experts on the disaster team, so he created the character of Makoto Aoyama (Masami Nagasawa), a meteorologist with a useful theory about King Ghidorah’s attraction to lightning storms. Godzilla Minus Zero has that typical sequel effect of moving away from a streamlined narrative toward a complicated one involving more monsters, more characters, more plotlines, more everything. There are promising story developments that aren’t fully explored and are presumably there as starter plotlines for sequels, such as the way living “Godzilla cells” are affecting humans, with a handful of scientific subjects who’ve survived contact with Godzilla but are now manifesting mutations. Noriko wears an eyepatch to cover her one reptilian yellow eye, and she also has Godzilla scales and spikes beginning to grow on one shoulder-blade, hidden by her clothing. Still, the film maintains that basic rhythm also remembered from childhood when watching old Godzilla films: big action scenes full of exciting destruction and terror interspersed with far duller but somehow reassuring meeting scenes when characters representing science, government, the military, and the model family unit regroup to try Plan B, Plan C, and so on. Yamazaki hasn’t come to challenge the genre conventions but to fulfill them and render them more beautiful. He makes vast CGI action sequences as sensational as it’s possible to make them, and it seems churlish to complain that, though generally magnificent, it’s still so much goddamn wearying CGI. It’s a generational viewership problem, really. I don’t think young people miss the sense of imprinting off of physical reality that once defined the film medium. But the figure of Godzilla has such lasting, surefire appeal, it’s hard to quell the basic moviegoer longing to see him again. As Yamazaki put it about his own lifelong obsession, As a kid, it was just: monster, cool, scary, amazing. Making these films now, I understand how much anxiety Japanese audiences were carrying when the first film came out in 1954, and how the monster’s shape matched that fear exactly. . . . Godzilla was never just a cool monster that wrecks things; he’s always carried the weight of the nuclear question, of war. The more I make these films, the more I feel that weight, and I think it’s exactly why people are still drawn to him. Godzilla brings his fear-shaped silhouette into contemporary times as we’re “drifting toward conflict” on a global scale, in Yamazaki’s view. He meant the sequel to be weightier and more complex: “It’s entertainment, but I wanted it to leave something heavy behind, too.” Yamazaki’s ability to unite fond nostalgia for Godzilla movies past, reaching back to childhood, with intensified modern angst forged in twentieth-century horrors that only grow over time, creates a riveting emotional combination. The third sequel is guaranteed, but it’s easy to imagine Yamazaki’s Godzilla movies maintaining their global appeal for as long as we’ve got a habitable globe to stand on. articles.title: Under Capitalism, Even Kids’ Playtime Is Alienated
articles.author: Evelina Johansson Wilén
articles.content: A central concern of feminist Marxist theory and practice has been how to understand the relationship between paid and unpaid labor. Marxist feminists have drawn on Karl Marx’s observation that capital leaves workers to ensure their own reproduction, a process that depends on their instinct for self-preservation. They have shown how capitalist accumulation depends on reproductive labor, work that has fallen primarily to women. But what, exactly, is being reproduced? Workers must replenish their strength so that they can work again the next day; importantly, reproduction also encompasses bearing children and creating future labor power. But it does not stop there of course: children must then be shaped into capable workers, a process that does not happen by itself and in which social reproduction is by no means simply left to the workers themselves. For anyone who has attended school, and perhaps even more so for those of us — myself included — who are now experiencing school all over again through our children’s education, it is more than apparent that school is, in many ways, an institution designed to socialize children into their future roles as wage workers. As E. P. Thompson writes in Time, Work-Discipline, and Industrial Capitalism , schooling can be understood as an acclimatization to the factory’s temporal discipline. Today, however, this involves more than the straightforward discipline Thompson identified. It also entails producing flexible, self-directed learners who can seamlessly retrain and acquire new skills in an ever-changing and volatile labor market. Playtime for Future Workers Despite this recognition of the importance of shaping working-class children in particular ways, children, and their role and position within capitalism, have remained marginal concerns within Marxist theory, as well as within feminist social reproduction theory. Perhaps this is precisely because children are not regarded as workers: neither productive nor reproductive. In her new book , Child’s Play: Childhood in and Against Capitalism , Susan Ferguson turns her attention to children, challenging the idea that they do not participate in reproductive activities. Ferguson argues that children are constantly involved in processes of creating and sustaining life, but primarily through play rather than through reproductive labor in any conventional sense. While Marxism has shown limited interest in children’s creative and life-sustaining activities, Ferguson argues that capitalism has a contradictory relationship with children, and particularly with children’s play. On one hand, the ideal of childhood as a sacred time for play, exploration, and curiosity emerged under capitalism and has since become firmly established. On the other, the regulation of children’s play, along with models from developmental psychology for determining whether play is age-appropriate, has become increasingly pronounced. Under capitalism, not only schooling but play itself becomes a preparation for the future. In this way, play acquires a kind of constructive dimension, with a clearly defined purpose, rather than being something free and open-ended, with no explicit goal beyond the sheer satisfaction that play itself provides. Learning to play properly becomes part of learning to work. In this sense, we are dealing with a form of alienated play. Beyond learning to play properly, it is also important to learn how to stop playing: to make the transition from being a “player” to being a “worker.” Children who deviate from the expected developmental trajectory, or who fail to acquire certain abilities according to an imagined timeline, quickly become targets of intervention. It is partly against this backdrop that we can understand the dramatic increase in ADHD diagnoses and other neurodevelopmental diagnoses that we are witnessing around the world. Children who cannot seamlessly adapt to the routines of school, whose minds wander during lessons, who are too lively or struggle to sit still, children who want to play rather than work, become problems to be solved, sooner rather than later. The Power of Play But what problem is solved by these interventions? Rates of depression and burnout are particularly high among women aged forty to fifty who work in health and social care. Women experiencing these problems are often medicated them rather than offered changes to their working conditions — changes that would require a redistribution of economic resources. Following a similar logic, instead of creating a school system that does not systematically produce failure, children are increasingly medicated so that they can cope with school. More than one in ten boys aged ten to seventeen in Sweden has an ADHD diagnosis . Surely this should prompt us to reconsider what counts as normal, and to place the school system that sustains this state of affairs under scrutiny, rather than focusing on how individual children can be helped to integrate into this abnormal normality? But Ferguson’s book is not only about how play has become subject to capitalist control; it is also about how children’s play can be understood as a site of resistance to capitalist logic. Although children’s games can, of course, be cruel, exclusionary, and governed by clear norms, Ferguson nevertheless sees the possibility of something transformative in children’s play. She describes this as “the embodied capacities of imagining and acting on and in the world in ways that fulfill our needs while nurturing human connections to the self, others and our environments.” Just as play can be utopian in its creation of new worlds, political organizing can also adopt a playful — that is, open-ended — attitude toward what might become possible. This does not mean that we can play capitalism to pieces, but that we can resist capitalism’s attempts to instrumentalize our creative impulses. Despite attempts to curb children’s play, whether through direct intervention or by restricting it to specific times, the games children play cannot be understood as exclusively capitalist or alienated activities. Rather, they can be seen as practices grounded in the sheer pleasure of playing, in the possibility of exploring, imagining and creating together without the activity necessarily having to lead to anything beyond itself. In this sense, play holds the potential to elude the capitalist logic that seeks to make every activity productive, measurable, and purposeful. Perhaps it is precisely in this openness, in the unpredictability of play and its capacity to imagine other ways of being together, that its political potential lies. Remember that you were once a child. This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture.
