articles.title: France’s “Hot Autumn” Is Boosting the Left
articles.author: Stathis Kouvelakis
articles.content: Since mid-September, a wave of protest has swept across France. High school students in working-class banlieues (suburbs) and the overseas territories started it by occupying their schools. University students, teachers, trade unionists, and a new generation of yellow vests ( gilets jaunes ) soon joined them. On November 5, about 1.6 million people took to the streets in two hundred cities. Emmanuel Macron’s government has answered with the harshest crackdown in half a century. Police have arrested more than ten thousand people, most of them teenagers. A new “Rioters Pay” bill would punish protesters for acts they did not personally commit. Meanwhile, the far right is stoking a racist backlash, and, on October 23, a far-right gunman killed a young man in Trappes. Stathis Kouvelakis has lived in France for more than four decades and has seen nearly every youth revolt there since the 1980s. In a wide-ranging interview with the editorial board of Jacobin Greece , he explains what makes this movement new, and why its young protesters are rallying around the idea of a “New France.” He also discusses the role of Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s La France Insoumise (LFI) and why the uprising could reshape next year’s presidential election and the European left. Jacobin How would you assess the state of the movement after October 17 and the government’s response? Stathis Kouvelakis Let me clarify, first of all, that the movement did not begin on October 17 but at least a month earlier, with the mobilization of school students. In the initial phase, it gradually spread to universities, parents, and teachers, and subsequently to the militant wing of the trade unions. What we saw on October 17 was a shift in the composition and a further expansion of the mobilization, with the rapid entry of virtually the entire trade union movement, of young workers, and of the new yellow vests. October 17 marks a turning point, because on that day the mobilization took on the characteristics of a popular uprising. We saw attacks on public buildings, the looting of three thousand shops, and a section of demonstrators — a minority, but by no means negligible — determined to clash with the police. The media, as usual, gave these acts of violence from below enormous and disproportionate coverage. But we must first and foremost see them as a response to the violence from above. On the one hand, they are a reaction to police repression unprecedented in over fifty years. On the other hand, they externalize the systemic violence that a section of society endures daily — marginalized young people in multiracial working-class suburbs endure it to a particularly acute degree. To grasp the extent of the repression, let us look at some figures. In less than a month, and before October 17, the police arrested eight thousand people — more than in the first six months of the yellow vests’ protests (2018–19). Eighty-five percent of those arrested were under eighteen; 2,700 are facing prosecution, and the courts have handed down 2,300 “alternative sentences.” On October 17, police arrested 2,700 more people, prosecutors brought around a thousand before the courts, and judges have already sentenced 217 to prison. These are staggering figures. Added to this is the brutality with which the police dealt with the students’ actions from the very outset. The government’s line was that this was not a social movement with specific demands but “riots” (“violences urbaines”), mere instances of “disturbance of public order” to which the only appropriate response is repression. The result was those unbelievable scenes of police violence both outside and inside schools, and on the streets of cities across the country. The situation is similar to that of the extremely violent crackdown on the yellow vests in 2018–19, except that now the main target is young people age fourteen to eighteen. So far, police grenades have torn off the hands of at least three people, and five have lost eyes to “rubber bullets” that police fired from defensive ball launchers (LBDs). Dozens, perhaps hundreds, of others have suffered irreversible physical injuries. On October 3, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez declared on television that he had given the police “no instructions to exercise restraint.” He emphasized that the security forces “will make use of the full range of weapons at their disposal,” meaning the lethal grenades and LBDs. Jacobin How did Emmanuel Macron and the government react to the unrest on October 17? Are they stepping up repression, backtracking, or remaining unyielding, believing that the movement will fizzle out? Stathis Kouvelakis The sheer scale of the mobilization and the violent clashes that followed came as a shock to the government. It had clearly underestimated the scale of the demonstrations (550,000 according to police figures, 800,000 according to the trade unions) and had consequently deployed relatively limited police forces. According to numerous accounts, while they made extensive use of force against the demonstrators, these forces remained passive or kept their distance from the areas where looting was taking place. In any case, police brutality backfired on the government. The brutality of the crackdown helped radicalize and expand the mobilization, undermining the government’s narrative within families and more broadly across society. On the other hand, however, the continuous escalation of repression that we have been witnessing for a decade now is accustoming a section of French society to the indiscriminate use of state violence. It fuels demands for restoring “law and order” by any means. The far right exploits these demands for political gain, particularly when the situation itself appears to be spiraling out of the state’s control. This crackdown, however, failed to break the movement. The authorities banned demonstrations in forty towns and cities and imposed daily curfews in many central areas. Despite this, on October 24, the rallies and demonstrations matched the scale of the previous Saturday (420,000 according to official figures, 800,000 according to the trade unions). In many cities, and particularly in Paris, the marches were even larger than the previous week. And this was during school and university holidays, with the army guarding public buildings and special anti-terrorist units patrolling the streets. For October 31, Macron stated that the authorities would only permit demonstrations in the “outskirts” of cities, far not only from their centers but also from the urban fabric itself. This provocative stance and repressive headlong rush are signs of weakness on the part of a faltering state authority that sees the ground slipping from under its feet. Jacobin We see school students at the forefront of the movement. This is a new phenomenon — how do you explain it? Stathis Kouvelakis It is not unusual in the French context for students to spark a wider mobilization. In a sense, the degree of convergence between the youth and the workers’ movement is the key to the major uprisings that periodically shake French society and to the radicalism that characterizes them. What is new is that it is now high schools rather than universities that are at the forefront. A second innovation of this movement is that it originates in deprived areas rather than, as is usually the case, in high schools in city centers. This means that at the forefront are students from working-class backgrounds and the multiracial banlieues , where a large proportion of the population originates from postcolonial immigration. It is no coincidence that the first school occupations took place in high schools in France’s overseas territories (Mayotte, the Antilles, French Guiana), where the situation remains strongly colonial. We therefore have a dual dimension: class and race. Both directly affect a youth that experiences firsthand the consequences of the neoliberal steamroller and the structural racism that permeates state institutions, the labor market, and social relations more generally. We can say that this movement has, from the outset, been deeply anti-racist and has a clear perception of the interconnection between racism and class inequality. This is also the key to understanding the third innovation of this student movement: its level of politicization and radicalism. Let me share a personal testimony here. From the early 1980s, when I began my studies in France, I took part in or observed at close quarters almost all the youth protests. The scene I witnessed on October 6, during the first major march with widespread participation, was unprecedented. What struck me most was the ability of the school students to link their material demands for better study conditions with the broader issues of the day. Alongside material demands concerning study conditions (shortage of teaching staff, deteriorating buildings, a competitive admissions process for higher education), this youth puts forward opposition to racism, war, genocide, police violence, and the logic of profit. Everywhere there were Palestinian flags and scarves, slogans against the far right and police violence, and a rejection of the militarism encroaching on schools — all this in a combative atmosphere. I heard thousands of schoolboys and schoolgirls, who were clearly not members of any left-wing organization, chanting rhythmically “jeunesse déterminée et révolutionnaire” [“We’re a determined and revolutionary youth”]. Such a thing was unthinkable not only for my own generation, which grew up in the bleak 1980s (especially bleak in France) but also for those that followed. The explanation lies in the overall nature of youth politicization internationally and in the particular significance that communities originating from postcolonial immigration hold for these generations. This is why Palestine occupies such a central position. It is not simply a matter of solidarity with a distant cause, however important that may be. In the oppression the Palestinians suffer, this youth recognizes the racism that it confronts itself. And the unyielding resistance of the Palestinian people is a source of inspiration for their own resistance and way of life. Jacobin What other forces have joined the school student movement? Stathis Kouvelakis The qualitative leap took place on October 17. Two factors played a decisive role here. The first was the call from the new yellow vests, which began circulating on social media in early September, even before the school occupations broke out. Unlike last year’s failed “Bloquons tout!” (“Let’s block everything!”) call, this one had strong organization and above all deep social roots. We know from related reports that the initiative came from young people, mainly non-white men from the working-class suburbs of major cities — a group very different from the “historic” yellow vests. Nor, for that matter, was the choice of date a coincidence. It falls, of course, on a Saturday, just like the days of action during the 2018–19 yellow vests movement. But it also coincides with the anniversary of October 17, 1961, when, during the Algerian War, the police fired into a protest march by Algerians in central Paris, killing dozens and throwing the bodies into the Seine. The parallel with the 2018–19 movement lies in the grassroots way the action spread and in its repertoire: rallies and marches scattered across the city that organizers did not declare to the authorities. It also lies in the demands, which focus on the cost of living. Gas prices are extremely high, which places an overwhelming burden on the working classes, who generally live some distance from their workplace. The cost of living is, of course, a broader issue, as real wages have stagnated, and the quality and accessibility of public services have plummeted. In the run-up to October 17, the student movement and the brutal police repression it faced had created a confrontational atmosphere. In that climate, the call met with a remarkable response from young workers, particularly those in precarious employment and in multiethnic suburbs, but also among sections of the working class outside the scope of trade unions. Despite initial reservations, it ultimately mobilized a minority but significant section of the “original” yellow vests. We can say that the experience of that movement is now part of the shared code of social movements in France. We even saw schoolboys and schoolgirls wearing these yellow vests at the roadblocks students set up during school occupations and, to a lesser extent, at the marches. The second factor is the involvement of the trade union movement. The most militant sections had already joined the fray earlier in October, protecting and supporting the school occupations and marches. These were mainly local branches of the General Confederation of Labor (CGT) and Solidaires, and in some places Force Ouvrière. In Toulouse and elsewhere, we also saw school and university students heading to workplaces and calling on workers to take to the streets. On October 17, trade union participation became widespread, drawing in even the extremely moderate French Democratic Confederation of Labor (CFDT). We could say that there is now a powerful popular bloc on the streets opposing “Macron and his world” — that is, the neoliberal steamroller and the growing state authoritarianism. This is the moment when all the separate movements of the last decade finally crystallized and converged. Its driving force is the youth as the bearer of a qualitatively new political consciousness. Jacobin La France Insoumise (LFI) is supporting the protests and is once again in the firing line of the government, the far right, and the media who say it is instigating them. How do you assess the role of LFI at this stage? Stathis Kouvelakis Indeed, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu stated on October 1 that behind the student occupations lie “LFI and its proxies from the ultraleft ( ultragauche ).” Lecornu chose these words on purpose: “proxies” is the term the media and mainstream discourse use for Hamas and Hezbollah, which they regard as proxies of Iran. And the term ultragauche refers not so much to organizations of the extra-parliamentary left as to the constellation of anarchists and autonomist groups — that is, groups or individuals operating outside the institutional, and sometimes even outside the legal, framework. This vocabulary reveals the mindset of those in power, who view a mobilized society in warlike terms. For years, the ruling extreme center and the far right have targeted LFI, often with the complicity of sectors of the “soft left.” The reason is that LFI is the only significant political force that breaks the consensus on critical issues such as support for the genocidal Zionist state, police violence, Islamophobia and structural racism, and alignment with US and Western imperialism. It is essentially the only genuine opposition to the current order. For LFI, supporting the mobilization is a matter of course. It means something very concrete and practical: mass participation in the marches and protection of the occupied schools and marches by LFI’s grassroots as well as by its deputies and mayors. The iconic figure is Bally Bagayoko, the charismatic newly elected mayor of Saint-Denis. He stands in solidarity with the occupied high schools in his city, and police have repeatedly beaten him when he tried to shield the students from their attacks. Within the movement, at the marches and at the roadblocks set up by the students occupying schools, LFI is like a fish in water. The mainstream media are speechless every time they see young people and, more broadly, the crowds in the streets enthusiastically cheering the seventy-five-year-old Jean-Luc Mélenchon. It is not simply because of his position on this particular issue. LFI is the only organization that has articulated the issues we now see stirring up those who take to the streets. To put it another way, what we are seeing is a dialectical relationship between the movements and LFI. To borrow a fine phrase from Houria Bouteldja, we should see LFI as our “war booty,” the fruit of our struggles of recent decades. As for the other sectors of the Left, they are of little concern to society. The only exception, in a sense, is the candidate of the Socialist Party and its allies, Raphaël Glucksmann, who represents the most right-wing, warmongering, and pro-US element within this part of the political spectrum. At every public appearance, people boo him, particularly young people, and he conspicuously stays away from any demonstrations. In his latest statements, he has endorsed the government’s so-called concessions. In essence, he is nothing more than a variant of Macron. I should also point out that Macron does not even have a working majority in the National Assembly. The successive governments he appoints survive solely thanks to the Socialists, who refuse to support the motions of no confidence that LFI, the Greens, and the Communists have introduced. Jacobin What is this “New France” that LFI speaks of? Has a new, multiracial subject of struggle and demands come to the fore? Stathis Kouvelakis “New France” is both a statement and an interpellation, or a call to action if you prefer. At first sight, it refers to the profound changes that French society has undergone in recent decades. The first is the end of the traditional countryside, and with it of the peasantry as a significant social group. The second is the internal migration that followed and continues to this day, albeit in a different form. Today one in two inhabitants of the country lives in a different area from that of their birthplace. But of course, “New France” refers above all to people with migrant origins, the overwhelming majority of whom are now French nationals. If we go back three generations, one third of the population has at least one non-French ancestor. France is a country with a tradition of immigration dating back to the very beginnings of the Industrial Revolution and even more so since the late nineteenth century. From the 1960s onward, however, the origin of this immigration shifted from Southern and Eastern Europe to the Global South, and in particular to the former French colonies of North and sub-Saharan Africa. Today, 20 percent of those under the age of eighteen are descendants of immigrants, and 84 percent of them are of non-European origin. However, as we know, this section of the population, despite being French citizens, faces persistent racist discrimination, which has intensified in recent years and taken the form of escalating Islamophobia. Many laws create an atmosphere of permanent suspicion against Muslims and deprive them of any form of independent organization. Furthermore, until recently, the French left — with the partial exception of the trade unions — had stubbornly refused to recognize this group as an integral part of its social base. It did so even though it constitutes the “hard core” of the working class. LFI recognizes racism not as an individual moral failing but as a mechanism of domination and exploitation that permeates all social relations. It speaks openly about the racist nature of police violence, of the labor market, and of an entire body of legislation that targets Muslims. In doing so, it turns a new page in the history of the French — and perhaps the European — left and its relationship with the working classes. One immediate result is the overwhelming share of the vote it is securing in the multiethnic working-class districts of the major cities, in the region of 60 to 70 percent. According to estimates , 70 percent of Muslims voted for Mélenchon in the first round of the 2022 presidential elections, and this figure is likely to be even higher in the next elections. Since the beginning of last year, New France has taken center stage in the discourse of Mélenchon and LFI. They now couple this observation with a call: those whom racism targets are not (merely) victims. They are, first and foremost, political subjects whom LFI calls on to take part in — and indeed to be at the forefront of — the struggle for social upheaval. At the impressive rally on June 7 in Saint-Denis (26,000 people), which launched LFI’s election campaign, the colorful — and largely youthful — crowd spontaneously chanted “New France,” waving French flags. The rally ended, as usual, first with the Marseillaise and then, at the crowd’s initiative, with the Internationale . However, New France ’s “baptism by fire” in mass action was undoubtedly this current movement. On the streets, and particularly in the student blocs and in front of the occupied high schools, the French flag was emphatically present, often alongside the Palestinian flag or those of other countries where Gen Z is rising up. Strong references to the French Revolution and its symbols accompany the tricolor. In the face of the far right’s racism and chauvinism, young people are putting forward a different France — one that reflects its people and their revolutionary traditions. It reflects the people as they are and as they constantly remake themselves through their struggles. The current situation marks the convergence of the political force of New France with a mass movement that is rallying an emerging popular bloc with majority support and a radical left-wing orientation. This is a historic moment, the moment when a new conception of the nation is emerging through the very action of the subordinate classes. In my view, far from contradicting a class-based hegemonic politics, New France paves the way for its reconstruction. The reason is simple: it is the only proposal capable of shattering racial divisions within the French working and popular classes. Only it can open up the possibility of uniting them into a new “historical bloc” — a force capable of leading society and giving it a radically new direction. It is also clear that this is the antithesis of nationalism and nostalgia for colonialism. As for LFI, its core position is that New France means a “de-Westernized” (“désoccidentalisée”) France. That France would have an independent foreign policy, breaking with the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and the imperialist framework and forging an alliance with the progressive forces of the Global South. It also means coming to terms with France’s colonial past and immediately recognizing the right to full self-determination of the people of Kanaky/New Caledonia. The New France project embodies the “ internationalist patriotism ” of Houria Bouteldja, a prominent figure in the de-colonial, anti-racist, and anti-imperialist movement in France. Jacobin How is the uprising affecting the wider political landscape? Stathis Kouvelakis It is still too early to have a clear picture, but a reasonable assessment is that such a development will intensify the existing social and political polarization. LFI is emerging as the natural political representative of the popular movement bloc, but on the other hand we are also seeing the formation of a “law and order” bloc, with Marine Le Pen’s National Rally as its main component. Two Frances are heading toward a frontal clash. The far right and its supporters, whose influence objectively extends into sections of the extreme center, are railing against the “unrest.” They blame it on “Arabs,” “blacks,” and “Islamo-leftists” — that is, the supposed unholy alliance between Islamists and LFI. The incidents that took place on October 17, and in particular the looting, provided ammunition for far-right rhetoric to denounce the actions of the “barbarians” — that is, the non-white youth of the working-class suburbs. The tragic culmination of this line of reasoning was the deadly attack on October 23 in Trappes, a working-class suburb on the outskirts of Paris. A thirty-nine-year-old fascist, driving around in his car, began shooting at non-white passersby who had the misfortune to be in his path. He killed a young man and seriously injured seven others, including an eleven-year-old girl. The perpetrator, who kept a copy of Adolf Hitler’s Mein Kampf at his home, stated that he had targeted “black people, Arabs, and Muslims” to “take revenge for the shopkeepers who lost their livelihoods on October 17.” An initial response to the far-right escalation came in recent days, when mayors and local organizations initiated a series of rallies and marches in working-class suburbs. But the most effective response is a mass presence on the streets in the coming days and, on a political level, the hegemonic momentum that the call for a New France has generated. Jacobin What do you think is now at stake for LFI? Stathis Kouvelakis LFI has so far succeeded in forging an organic relationship with the movement in terms of its agenda, its central narrative, and the participation of its grassroots. The challenge now is to offer a perspective that goes beyond the immediate task of the day, namely the mass mobilization for Mélenchon’s victory in next year’s presidential election. Here, however, lurks a difficulty. LFI is not a traditional party but a “movement.” In practice, this means there are no formal members; an online registration is sufficient to join a local “action group,” which enjoys a great deal of autonomy in practical matters. The organizational structure remains very loose, although for the past three years LFI has put coordinating structures in place at a regional level. This porous structure facilitates communication with the movements and respects their autonomy. However, it does not allow for coordinated intervention within them. Everything relies on the initiative of the grassroots, which naturally varies from place to place. It is, of course, entirely reasonable and correct to avoid the well-known pretension of “leading” movements by self-appointed “vanguards” and bureaucratic apparatuses. On the other hand, however, this does not help overcome the barrier that social movements have come up against throughout the recent historical period, and not only in France. That barrier is the challenge of forming a structure that gives them durability, cohesion, and the capacity for strategic autonomy. The question that arises is: How can we combine the autonomy of movements with the necessary, distinct intervention of political actors? The problem is by no means new. Nevertheless, it remains one of the most critical issues that not only LFI but also the radical left internationally must resolve — bearing in mind that every approach so far has failed. Jacobin What are the prospects for the uprising from here, and what are the next key dates? Stathis Kouvelakis November 5 was a milestone for the movement. About 1.6 million people took to the streets in two hundred cities across the country. The strike had a significant impact in some sectors, such as education, the civil service, the railways, and oil refineries. However, it did not grow into an all-out strike. The demonstrations were particularly impressive and joyful, bringing together young people and workers from various sectors. There is now a sense that a more cohesive popular bloc is emerging, carrying a novel and creative protest culture with its own music, scenography, and slogans. The government has responded with a simulacrum of negotiations on the one hand and a new escalation of repression on the other. It has offered some insignificant concessions, such as a €25 rise in the minimum wage and a minor modification of the admissions procedure for higher education. The only success the government can claim on that front is that it has split the union movement. The more moderate confederations, such as the CFDT and Force Ouvrière, have refused to call for further action. But the CGT, the teachers’ union Unitary Union Federation (FSU), and other important unions such as Solidaires and the National Union of Autonomous Trade Unions (UNSA) have called for a new day of street protests and strikes on November 17. The real purpose of those concessions is to cover up the hardening of police repression and of the legislation on street demonstrations. Since the schools reopened, police have intervened to prevent any form of occupation. The authorities are also asking principals to provide lists of students involved in the movement. University authorities have kept campuses affected by protests closed, some since late September, drastically reducing the possibilities for organizing mass action there. The government has also introduced a “Rioters Pay” bill in parliament. It would hold individuals liable for acts they did not personally commit, provided they “knowingly” took part in a gathering where acts of violence or property damage took place. The penalties are heavy: up to three years in prison and a €45,000 fine. Furthermore, the bill would allow the state to seize benefits that families of children involved in these actions receive and to expel foreign nationals whom courts find guilty of those offenses. The Senate has already approved the bill, and the National Assembly will now debate it. If parliament adopts it, the bill would “enshrine in law France’s shift toward authoritarianism,” as a petition launched by several well-known public figures puts it. Jacobin At a more strategic level, what is the movement’s political perspective? Stathis Kouvelakis What is really exceptional about this movement is that it is happening only months before next year’s presidential election, certainly the most decisive in half a century. The radical left, and LFI in particular, should see this as a gift from heaven. As historical experience suggests, only major social mobilizations can overturn the balance of political forces, both in society and at the ballot box. We should see the impressive momentum of Mélenchon’s campaign as the result of the movements of recent years, and the current movement will no doubt expand it even further. There is now a sense that a Mélenchon victory next year is a real possibility, albeit far from a certainty. In the streets and in everyday conversations among ordinary people, within families and groups of friends, one can feel this novel optimism. If Mélenchon wins, it will be a political earthquake of continental, even global, magnitude. But he will immediately have to confront an extremely hostile environment, both at home and internationally. The dominant classes have extremely powerful weapons at their disposal to strangle a government of the radical left. We have seen this happen many times in the past, in Europe and Latin America, and more recently in Greece in 2015. To survive this ordeal, the Left needs a confrontational line that mobilizes its own social base. The current situation in France provides these elements: broad sectors of society with an experience of mass action and a political force with a radical program and a real chance of electoral success. LFI calls this strategy a “citizens’ revolution.” I would prefer the term “democratic road to socialism,” which the late Nicos Poulantzas theorized. But the substance, I think, is quite similar: the articulation of a struggle within the state with mass movements that develop autonomously and push a left-wing government in a more radical direction. Once again, France appears as the laboratory for the European left. It is the only country where a force of the radical left can defeat the far right. It is also the only country, for the moment, that can initiate a process of social change capable of shifting the international balance of forces and opening up new possibilities for the Left worldwide. articles.title: Blue Wave Rejected Trump
articles.author: Erin Aubry Kaplan
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. The historic shellacking voters delivered to President Donald Trump and the GOP Tuesday already has many names — stinging rebuke, rejection, repudiation, reset. Analysts’ consensus is that the blue wave was a response to what so many Americans could see and feel every day — soaring prices, the effects of a needless war, blatant corruption at the top, all led by an erratic and increasingly unpopular president who openly dismissed the concerns of average people. The message was: enough. For anyone alarmed about the country’s Trump-led decline, the midterm results are beyond heartening, the best possible outcome. At the very least — and this is still huge — a Democratic takeover of Congress puts a serious check on the chaos. At most, it is a generational opportunity to change direction. But what remains undiscussed is what the election results will mean for the country’s most intractable and corrosive problem, what powered the rise of Trumpism 10 years ago and powers it still: racism. Will Democrats insist the country reembrace diversity? And if so, how? In the last two years, many norms have been degraded and discarded with astonishing speed, chief among them the ideal of racial equality that is at the heart of America itself. Undoing diversity, equity and inclusion programs was the first agenda item of Trump’s second term, because it was dear to his base, but more importantly, because he intuited that dividing the country racially would weaken it and make it vulnerable to his authoritarian ambitions. In his overarching campaign against DEI, Trump crossed lines and broke norms in ways detrimental and devastating for people of color, from sweeping federal job cuts that disproportionately hit Black workers to the targeting of Haitian immigrants for deportation to the recklessness and violence of ICE. It was the contempt and anything-goes lawlessness white authorities perpetrated on Black people during a century of Jim Crow segregation, but with the whole country drawn in this time. Were the midterms a repudiation of this? Dorian Warren, co-president of the civil rights organization Community Change, is cautiously optimistic they might be. When we spoke in 2016 Warren told me that the crisis of Trump’s election was racial, a white problem that only white people could ultimately resolve. While that hasn’t happened, he now thinks the midterm results are a mark of notable progress. “Though there were multiple motivations for voters, this was a definitely repudiation of Trump and MAGA,” Warren said in an interview on Thursday. “Think about it — now we have five Black governors. Keisha Lance Bottoms is the first Black female governor in history . . . It’s astounding.” Related: Destination Crenshaw: Can a $150 Million Art Project Save Black Los Angeles? Warren said that this could be the moment that the Democratic Party finally realizes the magnitude of debt it owes to Black voters, who turned out in force, especially across the South. “It’s like we’re saying, ‘Enough! We saved your butt many times,’” said Warren. “‘Stop running away from race.’” In other words, Democrats need to unapologetically own the diversity of their party, and of America itself. While it isn’t yet clear how much antiracism factored into the Democrats’ sweeping victory, there is no doubt about the role of Black Americans in pushing back. Black voters turned out in big numbers and shifted markedly to the left compared to 2024 . That is at least in part an angry reaction to the GOP’s bald attempts to wipe out Black political representation with gerrymandering that disappeared Black-majority districts after the Supreme Court’s latest gutting of the Voting Rights Act. That was perhaps the sweetest victory of all on Tuesday: that not only was a racist strategy ineffective, it backfired. Remarkable as that was, it’s also consistent with the resolve that has long characterized Black history. “It’s amazing how resilient we are,” said Warren. “They tried to shut us down, and we said, ‘No, we’re not doing this.’” Related: We Had Been Friends for 50 Years. Then We Had to Talk About Trump. Even if voters’ repudiation of Trump and the Republicans wasn’t chiefly about their racism, it was about morality. Candidates from Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico to Kansas Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton spoke about restoring decency, humanity and neighborliness to politics and American life. Talarico is a Presbyterian seminarian and Hamilton a Methodist pastor, but you didn’t have to be Christian to call out the moral rot of the Trump era, or to hear the message. While few white candidates actually talked about racism — Talarico has called Christian nationalism “fundamentally un-Christian” and racism “immoral and wrong” — Democrats have generally been reluctant to talk in detail about spirituality or race. The moment demands they do both. But even if the Democratic Party leaders don’t step up, Warren believes people of color will. “My first thought after the election was, ‘This is a rainbow coalition,’” he said. “People are calling the increase of Black and Latino Democratic voters ‘blacklash’ and ‘brownlash.’ But that’s a coalition.” While the Latino voters’ shift away from Trump was crucial, Warren said Black voters remain the anchor of the Democratic coalition. The question is whether their status within the party will change from being “captured” — taken for granted — to being “anchors” involved with directing the party and its mission. The answer has great implications for the larger existential question about whether the U.S. will finally decide to champion its diversity as a permanent political and cultural good. Even at this moment of uncertainty and inflection, those answers are probably not coming anytime soon. That’s fine with Warren. “As Black organizations and activists, we can’t wait around,” he said. “Now is the time we have to make demands and apply pressure. We have to get to work.” Capital & Main

articles.title: Global Left Rising
articles.author: Vijay Prashad
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Europe’s streets remain aflame with a population angry about how their war economies have utterly ignored their own people. Across the Atlantic, a fierce mobilisation in Brazil and the United States produced election results that favour the good side of history, without their own potential being exaggerated. The reaction of people in the Americas and Europe at present is that the abysmal growth rates due to the low investment in their own countries results in households cutting meals, in young people postponing independent lives, and in workers earning wages that cannot meet their Strait of Hormuz inflation expenses. Even if an eventual lower rate of inflation eventually slows the price rise, the accumulated rise in prices remains; a lower rate of inflation does not restore the purchasing power already taken from working people. That is why they are mobilised onto the streets and into the voting booth. India’s farmers’ revolt and the cockroach movement of large parts of society are very much part of this shift in the needle of history toward justice and way from the ugliness of decades of counter-revolutionary policies (which are euphemistically otherwise called neoliberalism). A defeat for Trump The November midterm elections in the United States have deprived US President Donald Trump’s Republicans of control of both houses of Congress. Anger over living costs and the war against Iran helped break their support for Trump’s Make America Great Again (MAGA) coalition. The day before the election, Trump gave a press conference to speak about how he had authorised the clean-up of the Reflecting Pool in Washington, and the day after the election, he told the press about his plans for a White House ballroom and signed an Executive Order to protect his decorations of the Oval Office. It appears that Trump has become the Interior Decorator-in-Chief with this defeat rather than the fierce MAGA leader that he had been. But this is misleading. Trump is capable of further aggression abroad and of cruelty at home to show that he is strong. The midterm election has exposed the weakened appeal of the MAGA bargain: workers are asked to finance military adventures while accepting insecurity as their personal responsibility. This is no longer of interest, but Trump must thump against popular opinion with his gargantuan ego operating with the belief that the MAGA constituency will never abandon him ultimately even if they turn against the Republican politicians. Related: India's Mediterranean Strategy: Warships, Billionaires, and NATO Democratic control of the US Congress creates opportunities for their largely unimaginative leadership to obstruct legislation, investigate the administration, and contest funding for Trump’s projects. Senator Charles Schumer and Congressman Hakeem Jeffries are like middle-management imperialists, unwilling to move against the status quo so willing to continue imperialist policies and at the same time to appear as if they care about the popular distress. Previous Democratic administrations helped to construct the machinery of US imperialism and have repeatedly defended it. Trump continues to command the armed forces, and so if he wishes to bomb Iran again, for instance, it is unlikely that a Democratic leadership, deferential to Israel, would object. There are now eight Democratic Socialist of America backed representatives in the US House, and there are several people who have openly opposed the Israeli genocide against the Palestinians and the US illegal war on Iran. They will need robust popular movements to draw upon the distress and anger of the population to turn an electoral rebuke into pressure against war, deportations, and attacks on social provision. Without such sustained pressure, the political establishment in the United States is very capable of absorbing the anger and continuing with much of the same policy. Eternal Lula Brazil offers the clearest defensive victory against the international far right of a special type. On October 25, Lula defeated Flávio Bolsonaro with 51.79 per cent of valid votes, winning his fourth presidential term, while Bolsonaro fled by private plane from Brazil to Miami in the United States. Lula’s victory blocks the return of the Bolsonaro family to the presidency and preserves space for struggles over wages, hunger, public investment, and national sovereignty. Internationally, it keeps Brazil available as an important voice against unilateral coercion and for cooperation among developing countries. A Bolsonaro victory would have strengthened the forces seeking to subordinate the region to Washington. The narrow mandate and the far right’s capture of the legislature reveals the depth of Brazil’s political division. The reactionary far right retains a substantial popular base, and an electoral victory – as Lula found the previous three times – cannot dissolve the power of agribusiness, conservative institutions, finance, and the harsh media. The far right having consolidated across the Americas leaves Brazil, Mexico, and Cuba as islands amid an ugly storm. That is why Lula’s renewed mandate cannot be judged merely by the election results but must be seen considering the material improvements in people’s lives. Defending democracy requires an economic programme that gives workers reasons to defend it. If the poor are asked only to protect institutions while their own needs remain postponed, the right will return to exploit their disappointment and redirect it against the left. Africa on the move Across Africa, where the median age is very low, mass protests of young people have consolidated into some important victories: the Gen Z uprising in Kenya (2024, 2025, 2026), the #EndBadGovernance protest in Nigeria (2024), the march to Parliament in Uganda (2024), the #StopGalamseyNow in Nigeria (2024), the post-election protests in Mozambique (2024-25), the youth protests in Togo (2025), the GenZ 212 in Morocco (2025), and the Gen Z Mada in Madagascar (2025) express the rhythm of the protest wave. These uprisings have faced twin reactions, meagre concessions and harsh repression, including long-term imprisonment for the leaders. The failure of the uprising in Tunisia and Egypt in 2011 hangs heavily over the youth, who protest but worry about the impossibility of change. The fulfilment of popular aspirations requires organisations able to resist both external financial discipline and the domestic concentration of power. That much is known, but from where will this organisation emerge. Related: The Red Sea War Economy: How Foreign Powers Profit While Africa Suffers South Africa’s Communist Party (SACP) is the most important left force on the continent, which is why its decision to contest the 4 November municipal election independently offers a new possibility for the African left. For the first time since the democratic breakthrough of 1994, the SACP sought votes under its own name, giving working-class discontent a distinct electoral expression. The Party has won over 700,000 votes, 2.38% of the total, and has won 261 seats (with high support in the Eastern Cape – 97 seats – and in Limpopo – 54 seats). The campaign asserted that workers and the poor must exercise their own political initiative within the unfinished struggle for national liberation, unfinished because of the dry taps, the unreliable electricity, the high rate of unemployment, and municipal decay. To build these electoral gains into durable popular power will require sustain mass work, including an expansion of the People’ Red Caravan, a form of cooperative building across the country. General Secretary Solly Afrika Mapaila has proposed bringing together left formations to discuss a common agenda, recognising that electoral representation must strengthen a wider movement. Popular forces need organisations capable of connecting immediate grievances to a programme that challenges the power of capital. Communist councillors will be judged by their ability to strengthen those struggles and make working people participants in the decisions that shape their lives. A renewed SACP will provide the leadership necessary across Africa for the consolidation of an African left to guide the popular uprisings against both exploitation and demoralisation. Europe’s burning streets France’s renewed mobilisation, building on the Yellow Vest movement of 2018 and the student struggles in intervening years, shows a route by which the working class is converging around the issue of wages, education, public services and the right to protest (including for Palestine). The energy has been infectious, moving to Italy’s October 30 strike and rolling unrest in Germany over conscription. Governments of Macron, Mertz, and Meloni quickly find money for armaments while insisting that schools and hospitals must accept scarcity. For now, all eyes are on the French presidential election, when the left will likely coalesce to challenge both the far right and the less far right. That is precisely the picture in Serbia, where the Student Lists’ won in the parliamentary elections with 140 of 250 seats against 103 for the list led by incumbent president Aleksandar Vučić. The movement grew after the deadly collapse of the Novi Sad railway station canopy in November 2024, which became a symbol of corruption and official impunity. Speculation about who backs this movement fails to see that it is built out of genuine grievances that have gathered wider anger into a sustained challenge to entrenched authority. The Serbian movement now faces the question confronting many youth uprisings: how to build durable democratic organisation and meet social needs after the exhilaration of mobilisation. Its victory nevertheless supplies encouragement to those told that powerful governments, protected by patronage and intimidation, cannot be removed through collective action. Protest led to parliament and now sets the Student List a serious task of driving a genuine social democratic agenda in a country cannibalised by European Union fiscal rules and by the corruption of its domestic elite. Related: Beyond Gaza's Rubble: How Israel Controls Palestinian Land, Water, and Money Israel’s Palestinian Trap Israel’s October 27 election delivered a serious setback to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, wanted by the International Criminal Court for war crimes. His bloc won 53 of the Knesset’s 120 seats, below the 61 required for a majority. Other Jewish parties have won 48 seats, also unable to build a stable government. The real surprise was delivered by the 900,000 Palestinian voters, who gave the Arab List groups 19 seats. The Palestinians voted against the genocide and now hold an opening against their political marginalisation in Israel. To form a stable government of the opposition would require their support, which then would mean that Palestinian issues are on the table. The election punished Netanyahu. It did not change the structure that benefits from the occupation of the Palestinian lands, the apartheid conditions of life for Palestinians, and the genocide in Gaza. The progressive potential in the election depends on whether pressure inside and outside Israel can secure Palestinian rights and halt the machinery of destruction. For that, there needs to be a global demand – as the International Peoples Assembly has said – for the Palestinians to have a right to political activity. The slogan will have to be extended from end the genocide to allow Palestinians to be political. Openings The crisis of our times does not choose its political outcomes. Insecurity amongst billions of people has indeed created the space for reactionary ideas and the movements of the far right of a special type. But this insecurity can also produce solidarity and resistance, indeed it can provide a start for social transformation. Electoral setbacks for dangerous governments create these openings that popular organisation must widen. The needle of history has moved because people have acted. Its further movement will depend on whether they can turn scattered refusals into sustained power over the decisions that govern their lives. Counterpunch

articles.title: The Republic on Trial
articles.author: Peter McLaren
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. On November 9, 2026, six days after the midterm elections, Donald Trump returned to a familiar accusation. Democrats had achieved what commentators were calling a blue tsunami, capturing control of both chambers of Congress and making substantial gains in states and districts that had long been regarded as Republican strongholds. Trump had initially indicated that he would accept the results. On election night, he told The New York Times that he was “absolutely willing” to do so. In an interview broadcast by CBS's 60 Minutes on November 8, he acknowledged the Republican losses and offered his explanation: he had not been on the ballot, and voters were unhappy with the economy and the war in Iran. The following day, however, he changed course. “Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest,” he wrote on Truth Social. “How could the Polls be so wrong??? Some early voting ‘dumps’ were so large that it was impossible to win, no matter how many people went to vote. It’s all about the machines, which are far more important than the voter!” The final sentence was particularly consequential. Trump did not identify a particular voting machine, produce evidence of altered ballots, or demonstrate that any machine had miscounted votes. But by invoking voting machines while questioning the honesty of the election, he again placed the integrity of the electoral process under suspicion. The accusation was not accompanied by evidence of widespread fraud or wrongdoing. Election officials had raised no major concerns about early voting or voting machines in the 2026 races. There was another problem with his complaint about the polls. Public surveys had broadly anticipated a Democratic wave. They had not necessarily predicted the full magnitude of the victories, but the direction of the results was hardly inexplicable. The electorate had delivered its judgment, and the available evidence did not substantiate Trump's insinuations about the machinery of the vote. The sequence is worth remembering. On election night, Trump said he would accept the results. Six days later, after the scale of the Republican defeat had become unmistakable, he questioned their honesty. Related: Trump, the Imperial Presidency, and the Perilous Future of the Republic This is not an isolated episode. It recalls a political pattern whose most consequential expression occurred after the presidential election of 2020, when Trump refused to accept defeat, advanced unsupported allegations of widespread fraud, and pursued an extraordinary effort to prevent the peaceful transfer of power. The calendar offers its own unsettling symmetry. On January 6, 2021, a violent crowd interrupted Congress's certification of Joe Biden's victory. On January 6, 2025, Congress peacefully certified Trump's own electoral victory. Now, in November 2026, the language of electoral suspicion has returned—not after a presidential defeat, but after the president's party suffered a sweeping midterm loss. To understand the significance of this moment, we must distinguish between changing votes and preparing to challenge an election; between legitimate scrutiny and unsupported allegations; between the right to contest a result and the obligation to accept evidence when the contest fails. The question is no longer confined to what happened in 2020, or what was prepared for in 2024. It concerns the durability of a republic in which the legitimacy of an election must not depend upon who wins. The Unfinished Business of 2020 The presidential election of November 2020 was followed not by a customary concession but by an escalating effort to reverse the result. Trump and his allies challenged results in battleground states, pressured state officials, promoted allegations of widespread fraud, and pursued legal strategies that failed in court. Recounts and audits did not substantiate claims of fraud sufficient to change the outcome. The effort extended beyond litigation. In several states, groups of Trump supporters signed certificates falsely purporting to represent legitimate presidential electors. These documents were part of a larger attempt to create an alternative account of the Electoral College vote. The pressure campaign also reached Vice President Mike Pence, whom Trump and his allies sought to persuade to reject or delay the certification of electoral votes. The congressional investigation into January 6 documented the extent of this effort. Its final report concluded that Trump's own campaign officials, Justice Department officials, and White House advisers had told him that his allegations of widespread fraud were false. Nevertheless, he continued to promote those allegations, pressured state officials to change certified results, and participated in efforts to transmit false electoral certificates to Congress and the National Archives. The report also documented Trump's pressure on Pence to refuse to count lawful electoral votes. Pence declined to do so. The constitutional significance of January 6, 2021, cannot be reduced to the violence of the Capitol attack, however shocking that violence was. The attack occurred within a broader political effort to obstruct the peaceful transfer of presidential power. The crowd that entered the Capitol interrupted the constitutional proceeding through which the result of the election was to be formally recognized. The courts rejected the principal legal challenges. State officials certified their results. Congress ultimately reconvened and completed the count. Yet the damage was not confined to the failed effort to retain the presidency. Trust in elections, public confidence in election administrators, and the security of those responsible for conducting elections had been placed under sustained pressure. The central lesson of 2020 was not merely that an attempt to overturn an election had failed. It was that the institutions of American democracy could be subjected to extraordinary pressure by a president unwilling to accept the judgment of the electorate. The Continuity of Personnel and Method The connection between 2020 and 2024 was not simply rhetorical. There were identifiable continuities in personnel and organizational practice. One particularly revealing example is Christina Bobb, a former Trump attorney who had been involved in efforts to challenge the 2020 election results, including the false-elector effort in Arizona. In March 2024, the Republican National Committee appointed Bobb as its senior counsel for election integrity. The Washington Post reported that Bobb remained in this position even after being charged in Arizona in connection with efforts to reverse the 2020 result. Her appointment was significant not because it proved that the 2024 election was to be manipulated, but because it demonstrated that a figure associated with the 2020 effort had moved into a prominent position within the party's formal election apparatus. Related: Elbows Up! Canada, Trump, and the Politics of Democratic Friendship The Republican Party was entitled to organize lawyers, recruit volunteers, monitor polling places, and challenge election procedures through the courts. Those activities are not inherently improper. Election integrity is a legitimate concern, and scrutiny of election administration is part of democratic accountability. But the political context mattered. Some of the people involved in the 2024 election operation had previously promoted claims about the 2020 election that were not supported by evidence. The organizational continuity deserved scrutiny, particularly when combined with the repeated suggestion that an unfavorable result could not be legitimate. The machinery of electoral distrust can be built without altering a single ballot. It can operate through public declarations, litigation, recruitment, political pressure, and the repeated suggestion that defeat is evidence of corruption. Preparing to Challenge the Result By the autumn of 2024, the Republican Party had assembled a substantial election operation. The campaign and the RNC pursued litigation over election rules and voting procedures, recruited volunteers to monitor elections, and prepared legal challenges that could be brought after the vote. Again, these activities must be described accurately. Filing lawsuits is not the same as falsifying votes. Poll watching is not inherently intimidation. Parties have a legitimate right to monitor the process and to seek judicial review when they believe election laws have been violated. The larger concern was the political context in which this operation developed. Trump repeatedly warned that the only way he could lose was through cheating. He urged supporters to deliver a victory “too big to rig,” while making unsupported allegations about noncitizen voting and other supposed avenues of electoral fraud. The effect of this rhetoric was to establish a political framework in which an unfavorable result could be treated as suspicious before the evidence had been examined. The distinction between rigging an election and preparing to contest its outcome is essential. The available record does not establish that the Trump campaign devised a plan to falsify ballots or alter the numerical outcome of the 2024 election. Trump won that election. The result was certified. But the preparations for legal and political challenges, when accompanied by repeated declarations that defeat could only result from cheating, raised a different question: Was the purpose merely to protect the integrity of the election, or was the public also being prepared to reject an unfavorable result? That question does not require us to assume that every lawyer or volunteer shared an improper purpose. It requires us to examine the documented statements, organizational relationships, and political conduct of those directing the operation. A democracy depends not only on the right to challenge an election, but also on the willingness to accept the outcome when the evidence does not support the challenge. The People Who Count the Votes The consequences of this political climate have been felt most directly by the people responsible for administering elections. A Brennan Center for Justice survey conducted in 2024 found that 38 percent of surveyed local election officials reported experiencing threats, harassment, or abuse because of their work. The survey also documented widespread concern about political interference and the safety of election workers and their families. These are not abstract constitutional concerns. Local election officials are the people who maintain registration records, supervise polling places, count ballots, certify results, and perform the often invisible work that makes representative government possible. Their independence is indispensable. When public officials and political leaders repeatedly cast doubt on election administration without evidence, the consequences reach beyond partisan disagreement. Election workers become targets. Some leave their positions. Others must consider the safety of their families. The ordinary administration of democracy becomes an act performed under intimidation. Related: Che Guevara, Paulo Freire, Cuba, and the Future of Hope A republic cannot function if the people who count its votes are expected to work under the threat of political retaliation. Nor can public confidence be restored simply by insisting that citizens trust the process. Trust must be sustained by evidence, institutional independence, transparency, and the willingness of political leaders to accept results they do not like. January 6, 2021—and January 6, 2025 The historical symmetry of January 6 is difficult to ignore. On January 6, 2021, Congress met to count the electoral votes confirming Joe Biden's victory. A violent crowd of Trump supporters stormed the Capitol, interrupted the proceedings, injured police officers, and threatened elected representatives and the vice president. The certification was delayed, but Congress eventually reconvened and completed its constitutional duty. Four years later, on January 6, 2025, Congress met again to certify the result of a presidential election. This time, Donald Trump had won. Vice President Kamala Harris presided over the proceeding and formally announced the result of her own defeat. Trump received 312 electoral votes; Harris received 226. No member of Congress objected to the results. The count was completed in approximately half an hour. The contrast was extraordinary. The candidate who had sought to overturn the previous election was now the beneficiary of a legitimate electoral victory. The candidate who had lost presided over the formal recognition of that victory. There was no violence, no mob, no interruption of the constitutional proceeding. The peaceful certification of 2025 was a necessary and welcome demonstration that the constitutional process could still function. But the contrast also raises a question that should not be evaded: Was January 6, 2021, an aberration, or did it reveal a vulnerability that remains unresolved? The peaceful proceedings of 2025 do not erase the events of 2021. Nor should the fact that Trump won in 2024 be used to retroactively validate the claims he made after losing in 2020. An election is not legitimate because the candidate whose victory was challenged eventually wins another one. Its legitimacy rests upon the rules, evidence, and constitutional procedures that govern every election, regardless of the identity of the victor. There was, however, an important institutional change between the two certifications. Congress passed the Electoral Count Reform Act in 2022, clarifying the vice president's limited role in the certification process and raising the threshold for congressional objections to a state's electoral votes. The law was intended to close vulnerabilities exposed in 2020. Such reforms matter. But legislation cannot by itself restore a political culture in which electoral defeat is accepted as part of democratic life. The law can establish procedures; it cannot compel political leaders to respect the principles that make those procedures meaningful. The Blue Tsunami and the Return of Electoral Suspicion The November 2026 midterms have added another chapter to this history. The Democratic victories were not confined to a handful of familiar battlegrounds. The party captured both chambers of Congress and made substantial gains across the country, including in states where Republican candidates had prevailed by considerable margins in 2024. The results produced a divided government and a new political reality for the remainder of Trump's presidency. A president is entitled to criticize election administration. He is entitled to request investigations, seek recounts, and present evidence of irregularities. The right to question government is not reserved for the opposition. Indeed, the credibility of democratic institutions depends upon their willingness to investigate genuine concerns. But allegations must be measured against evidence. Trump's November 9 statement did not identify a particular machine, jurisdiction, technical malfunction, or verified discrepancy. It did not offer evidence that votes had been altered. Election officials had not reported major concerns about the machines or early voting in the 2026 races. The public polling had broadly anticipated a Democratic wave, even if it had not fully captured its scale. The issue, therefore, is not whether election technology should be scrutinized. It should. Nor is it whether political leaders may challenge election procedures. They may. The issue is whether a president can repeatedly cast doubt upon the legitimacy of electoral outcomes without presenting evidence sufficient to support his accusations. When such claims come from the highest office in the country, they carry consequences. They can weaken public confidence in election administration, expose local officials to harassment, and encourage citizens to regard the counting of votes as a partisan enterprise rather than a constitutional responsibility. The 2026 statement also recalls the language of 2020. Then, Trump questioned the machinery of a presidential election he had lost. Now, after his party's midterm defeat, he has again invoked voting machines and questioned the honesty of the result. The circumstances are not identical. The 2020 effort involved a sustained campaign to reverse a presidential election, including pressure on state officials, false electoral certificates, and an attempt to obstruct congressional certification. The November 2026 statement, as of this writing, is a public allegation, not evidence of a comparable operational plan. We should not conflate the two. But neither should we ignore the recurring pattern: electoral legitimacy is called into question when the outcome is unwelcome. The Next Test: Congress and the Justice Department The midterm election has produced more than a change in congressional arithmetic. It has opened a confrontation over the constitutional authority of Congress to investigate the executive branch—and over the willingness of the administration to submit to that scrutiny. The conflict became unmistakable on November 7 and 8. As Democrats prepared to assume control of both chambers, President Trump denounced their proposed investigations as “extortion at the highest level.” He then went beyond public criticism. In a Truth Social post, he directed the Justice Department to investigate what he described as criminal conduct by Democratic lawmakers who had threatened investigations, impeachment, and other penalties against members of his administration. Attorney General Todd Blanche subsequently refused to rule out criminal investigations or prosecutions of Democratic lawmakers. On the Sunday political programs, he criticized their rhetoric and singled out Representative Robert Garcia, the California Democrat expected to chair the House Oversight Committee. Garcia had warned administration officials to “lawyer up” in anticipation of congressional inquiries. Related: Revolutionary Prophetic Pedagogy: Reclaiming Schools for Democracy in an Age of Oligarchy The details matter. According to Axios, Blanche did not identify a specific criminal statute that the lawmakers might have violated, nor did he confirm that the Justice Department had opened an investigation in response to Trump's directive. The Washington Post likewise reported that Trump had ordered the department to examine Democrats who had pledged to scrutinize his administration. The distinction between a presidential instruction, an actual investigation, and a prosecutable offense must be maintained. Nevertheless, the constitutional implications are serious. Congressional oversight is not, by itself, extortion or criminal conduct. It is one of the principal means by which the legislative branch holds the executive accountable. Congress has authority to investigate matters relevant to legislation, public expenditure, and the conduct of government. That authority is not unlimited, and individual lawmakers are not exempt from generally applicable criminal law. But the prospect of investigations, subpoenas, or impeachment proceedings cannot automatically be treated as criminal merely because the administration objects to them. The incoming Democratic majority has promised to examine a range of issues involving the administration, including its use of the Justice Department, its treatment of political opponents, immigration enforcement, and alleged conflicts of interest and corruption. Such inquiries will require evidence, procedural fairness, and discipline. Oversight must not become a substitute for proof, nor should impeachment be invoked as a partisan reflex. But the executive branch cannot claim immunity from investigation simply because the questions are politically inconvenient. The Washington Post reported on November 8 that the Justice Department was preparing for an extensive wave of congressional scrutiny after two years in which Republican congressional leaders had provided comparatively little oversight of the department's most contentious actions. Democrats are preparing subpoenas and investigative inquiries into the department's conduct during Trump's second term. The coming inquiries will examine, among other matters, the relationship between federal law enforcement and the White House. This confrontation is particularly consequential because the Justice Department occupies a position that demands institutional independence. Prosecutorial decisions should be grounded in evidence and law, not in the political interests or personal grievances of the president. When a president directs the department to investigate lawmakers who are preparing to investigate his administration, the appearance of a conflict between presidential interest and independent law enforcement becomes unavoidable. The administration has defended its position by arguing that lawmakers must not threaten private citizens, donors, or public officials with punishment simply because they hold opposing political views. Those concerns deserve examination where specific conduct is alleged. But the constitutional distinction remains: legitimate congressional oversight, including the investigation of executive officials and consideration of impeachment, is not rendered criminal by presidential objection. Here, the historical symmetry becomes difficult to ignore. After the 2020 election, Trump and his allies sought to enlist the Justice Department in efforts to challenge the result and retain presidential power. In the present confrontation, the department is being directed to examine lawmakers who intend to scrutinize the administration. The circumstances are not identical, and the facts must be assessed on their own merits. But in both episodes, the independence of federal law enforcement and its relationship to presidential power are central questions. The incoming Congress will have its own responsibilities. It must distinguish genuine misconduct from partisan accusation, protect the rights of witnesses, and ensure that investigations are grounded in evidence. It must also resist the temptation to turn oversight into spectacle. A congressional majority is not a license to presume guilt. But neither is the presidency a license to place the executive branch beyond scrutiny. The next test of constitutional government will therefore involve more than the conduct of elections. It will concern whether Congress can investigate the executive without intimidation, whether the Justice Department can exercise prosecutorial judgment independently, and whether the president can accept the constitutional limitations imposed upon his office. The republic's separation of powers was designed precisely for moments such as this. Its institutions are not supposed to protect those who hold power from accountability. They are supposed to make accountability possible. The Fragility of Democratic Consent The danger to democracy does not always arrive in the form of an unmistakable assault. Sometimes it develops through the gradual erosion of shared assumptions: that votes should be counted honestly, that evidence should matter more than accusation, that courts should be respected when they reject a claim, and that the peaceful transfer of power is not a privilege granted to the winning party but an obligation binding every participant. The events of 2020 demonstrated what can happen when those assumptions are abandoned. The preparations surrounding the 2024 election demonstrated how distrust could become embedded in a political organization's formal election apparatus. The peaceful certification of January 6, 2025, demonstrated that constitutional procedures can survive even after having been subjected to extraordinary strain. And the November 2026 statements and ensuing confrontation over congressional oversight have brought the question of constitutional accountability back into public view. These developments should not be collapsed into a single accusation. The 2024 election was not shown to have been stolen or falsified. Trump won it. The result was certified. The 2026 midterm results, too, have not been shown to involve widespread fraud or machine manipulation. Democrats won control of Congress. But the republic's health cannot be measured only by whether the machinery of government successfully completes its formal rituals. It must also be measured by whether political leaders respect the electorate when the electorate refuses them power; whether election officials can perform their duties without intimidation; whether Congress can exercise its oversight authority; and whether the Justice Department can distinguish the enforcement of law from the pursuit of political advantage. The issue is not whether a political leader who once challenged an election should be denied the opportunity to seek office again. The issue is whether the institutions of a republic can remain secure when the acceptance of electoral outcomes becomes conditional upon the identity of the winner. January 6, 2021, revealed the consequences of that condition in its most violent form. January 6, 2025, offered a moment of constitutional relief. November 9, 2026, reminds us that the underlying question has not disappeared. A republic is not sustained by the victory of one party over another. It is sustained by the willingness of those who lose to recognize that the people—not the president, not the party, not the movement—possess the final authority to decide who governs. And when the president himself questions the machinery by which the people have spoken, the burden is not on the electorate to prove that its voice was real. The burden is on the accuser to produce evidence. That principle is neither ceremonial nor negotiable. It is the unfinished business of American democracy. Selected Sources and Further Reading 1.
