articles.title: Air Traffic Controllers
articles.author: Brett Wilkins
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Air traffic controllers are rejecting US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s explanation for Friday’s nationwide flight ground stop, raising questions about the Trump administration’s account of a communications failure that disrupted air travel across the United States , affecting an estimated 1.5 million travelers. Washington Examiner homeland security reporter Anna Giaritelli told CNN’s Laura Coates during a Friday night interview that she’d spoken with 60 air traffic controllers about the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop, which was just the third to ever occur. “None of them are buying what he said,” Giaritelli said. “The controllers were saying, ‘We don’t buy that this is actually what’s happening, the reason that Sean Duffy is saying this has happened.’” View the original article to see embedded media. At a White House briefing Friday evening, Duffy blamed the disruption on America’s aging air traffic control infrastructure , saying overloaded switches and routers had produced inconsistent radar and communications data. “Our switches, our routers actually got overloaded with data,” he said. “And because of that, we shut the system down.” But Giaritelli said the controllers she contacted questioned the plausibility of the administration’s account, particularly the timing of the alleged equipment changes. “These types of switches... that the FAA is doing, they don’t happen during the day,” she told Coates. “They don’t happen during busy times like a Friday afternoon. They’re doing these midweek, middle of the night, when there is no air traffic going on.” Giaritelli’s comments came as the Trump administration struggled to explain how a failure in the nation’s air traffic control network could have escalated into a shutdown affecting airports nationwide. The FAA lifted the ground stop at approximately 8:15 pm Eastern on Friday, but the disruption continued Saturday. Duffy offered a new detail on Saturday, saying that a system overload occurred when contractor L3Harris Technologies Inc. was replacing a section of the air traffic control system’s old copper wire with new fiber wire. “Our contractor didn’t meet the moment or the equipment didn’t meet the moment,” the secretary said, adding that officials were investigating whether the contractor’s “incompetence” or a faulty router was to blame. Duffy emphatically denied that the FAA’s recent nationwide rollout of an $875 million artificial intelligence system called Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes, and Trajectories (SMART) had anything to do with Friday’s disruption, claiming that the system “is not even plugged in.” The FAA said earlier this week that it “will now use SMART in the airspace of all 22 [air traffic control] centers across the country to reduce delays, reduce fuel consumption, and improve the travel experience for the flying public.” Duffy also used the crisis to renew his demand for $50 billion in congressional funding to overhaul the nation’s air traffic control system, arguing that the aging infrastructure would continue to fail without additional investment. The administration’s shifting account has added to calls for an independent investigation. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Friday that investigators had found no evidence of a cyberattack, although he acknowledged that the possibility had not been entirely ruled out. Rep. James Walkinshaw (D-Va.) was among those who challenged the administration’s explanation, suggesting that Duffy had concealed the role of the Trump administration’s own modernization efforts. Walkinshaw cited a September report from the Government Accountability Office warning that precisely this could happen. . @SecMullinDHS seems to have revealed what @SecDuffy was trying to hide. Today’s ground stop was a result of the @realDonaldTrump air traffic control modernization work. pic.twitter.com/IMt3pwJmQe — Rep. James Walkinshaw (@Rep_Walkinshaw) November 14, 2026 “In essence, the FAA is buying delivery speed at the risk of cost uncertainty and potential disruptions,” GAO said. “The net effect could be that air traffic controllers are forced to continue to rely on severely outdated systems that are prone to failure leading to more system outages, ground stops, flight delays, or worse—safety incidents.” The fiasco prompted critics, including Democratic New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, to call for Duffy’s resignation. “From chronic air traffic controller shortages to repeated communications breakdowns, serious lapses in our aviation system have become a pattern on Sean Duffy’s watch,” Hochul wrote on Facebook. “Through it all, he’s been more focused on starring in his own reality show than addressing the crisis at his agency,” she added, referring to the former MTV “Real World: Boston” and “Road Rules: All Stars” participant’s “ The Great American Road Trip ” travel series, which features his family, including his wife, Fox News personality Rachel Campos Duffy. The ground stop was the longest nationwide aviation shutdown in 25 years, with more than 3,500 aircraft already airborne when the FAA ordered the grounding. More than 4,100 flights were canceled Saturday alone, according to FlightAware. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said Saturday that normal operations were expected to resume by Sunday evening.

articles.title: Questions to Ask Before Hiring an Injury Attorney
articles.author: Tiqua Jackson
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Finding the Right Personal Injury Lawyer After an Out-of-State Accident After an accident away from home, you may be dealing with an unfamiliar insurer, medical bills from another state, and questions about where to find a lawyer. The nearest office may not be the right place to start. Focus your search on these checks: Check authorization. Verify the attorney's licensing and ask how they would be authorized to handle your case. Test relevant experience. Use the first conversation to learn how the lawyer handles cases like yours. Understand the agreement. Get fee and expense terms in writing before you sign. This guide provides general information, not advice about your case. An appropriately authorized attorney can review your circumstances. Find Someone Who Can Handle the Case Where It Belongs If you were injured in another state, ask where your claim could be brought, which rules apply, and who may represent you there. Your home address alone won't answer those questions. Start with the location of the accident. Ask whether the claim could be brought in that state and what other locations might be available. For example, Michigan Legal Center's October 2026 explanation says whether a particular Michigan court can hear a case depends on the claim and the defendant's connections to Michigan. That example illustrates why a lawyer needs to review more than where you live. For an accident in New Jersey, an NJ injury lawyer such as Garces, Grabler & LeBrocq is an option to research. Confirm who would handle the matter and whether that attorney is authorized to appear in the relevant court. The firm lists motor vehicle accidents, truck accidents, and workers' compensation among its practice areas. Ask which type of claim fits your circumstances. Check the individual attorney. An office address alone doesn't establish whether the lawyer handling your file can appear in the relevant court. Look the individual up in that state's official directory. Maryland's attorney listing treats active status as good standing and authorization to practice, and the State Bar of Texas shows any public disciplinary history on each attorney's online profile. Licensing status doesn't establish experience with your type of claim. A lawyer licensed elsewhere may sometimes participate by working with a locally admitted lawyer who actively participates. The ABA model rules describe a conditional route for temporary legal services, but current state rules control. Ask how the proposed arrangement would work and whether separate court approval is needed. Request a deadline review early. Maryland has a default three-year filing period for civil actions at law, subject to other Code provisions. That rule does not establish the deadline for an out-of-state accident. Ask an attorney to identify when your filing period begins and which deadlines apply. Use the First Conversation to Test the Fit Use the consultation to learn how the lawyer would approach your claim and whether their working style suits your needs. Bring questions and take notes so you can compare the answers afterward. Bring a useful file. Gather a short timeline, photographs, witness names and contact details, the report number, insurance correspondence, and whatever medical and wage records you have so far. If you exchanged insurance details with the other driver at the scene, include those as well. Ask about cases like yours. Ask how often the attorney handles your type of accident, how they approach disputed responsibility, and what evidence they would gather. Ask what information they need before discussing a possible recovery. If your injuries are severe, ask about experience with long-term care needs. For serious injuries in Texas, Stogner Trial Law describes its catastrophic-injury category as life-altering injuries requiring extensive medical care and long-term support. Notice how answers are given. Ask who will handle the matter, how updates work, and what you can do from home rather than in person. Texas Court Help notes that one of a lawyer's most important duties is keeping the client reasonably informed about the status of the matter. Follow up by asking whom to contact with questions and how to send new records. Write down the proposed communication arrangements. Know What You Are Agreeing To Under a contingency-fee arrangement, the attorney's fee depends on a recovery. Expenses may be handled separately, so review both in the written agreement. Separate fees from expenses. The attorney's fee is one item; litigation expenses, such as records requests and expert reports, are another. Ask whether medical liens, or claims for repayment of medical costs, could also reduce what you receive. Review any firm's written agreement for the percentage and expense terms that would apply to your case. Texas Disciplinary Rule 1.04(d) requires contingent-fee agreements to be in writing and to state whether expenses are deducted before or after the fee is calculated. The order affects your share. Ask which method applies, what the percentage is, and whether it changes if the case goes to trial. Confirm the scope. Ask who is responsible for the case, whether another firm or local counsel may participate, and what work is included. If you are considering a firm for a serious injury claim, ask it to explain how its contingency arrangement applies to your matter, what case expenses you may owe, and who would handle the work. Use the same questions with every firm you compare. Read before signing. The ABA model fee rule calls for a written contingent-fee agreement signed by the client, though current state rules govern. Ask for explanations of any terms you don't understand, including what expenses, if any, you could owe without a recovery. Get the agreement in writing and keep a copy for your records. The same care applies later in the claim. Accepting a settlement usually means signing a release that bars future claims tied to the accident, so take your time with any offer and keep your statements to insurers calm and factual before agreeing to a number. Conclusion The right lawyer after an out-of-state accident is the one who can work where your claim belongs, has handled cases like yours, and explains the agreement clearly. Start by confirming that the attorney is authorized in the state where your case would be heard, then use the consultation to compare how each lawyer would approach your claim and keep you informed. Before you sign, make sure the fee percentage, the expense terms, and the people handling your file are all set out in writing. Taking those steps early protects your filing deadline and puts you in a stronger position for the rest of the claim. Frequently Asked Questions Do I need a lawyer licensed in the state where the accident happened? Usually, the attorney who appears in court on your claim needs to be authorized in that state. A lawyer licensed elsewhere may sometimes take part by working with a locally admitted lawyer, but each state's rules decide when that is allowed. Ask any firm you speak with how it would be authorized to handle your case. How do personal injury lawyers charge for their work? Many work on a contingency basis, which means the fee depends on a recovery. Case expenses, such as records requests and expert reports, may be handled separately. The written agreement should explain the percentage, how expenses are treated, and what you could owe if there is no recovery. What should I bring to a first consultation? Bring a short timeline of the accident, photographs, witness contact details, the police report number, insurance correspondence, and any medical and wage records you have. A complete file helps the lawyer assess your claim and gives you a fair basis for comparing firms. How long do I have to file a personal injury claim? Filing deadlines vary by state and by type of claim. Maryland's default period for civil actions at law is three years, and Texas generally allows two years from the date of injury for personal injury lawsuits. Because other rules can change the deadline, ask an attorney to confirm when your filing period begins. Should I accept the insurance company's first settlement offer? Take time to review any offer before agreeing to it. A settlement usually comes with a release that ends future claims tied to the accident, even if your injuries later turn out to be more serious. Make sure you understand the full extent of your losses before you sign.

articles.title: Laminate Flooring Durability
articles.author: Britta Hedlund
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Choosing new flooring can feel overwhelming, especially when vinyl and laminate look so similar at first glance. Both are budget-friendly, stylish, and widely available — but they're not the same when it comes to lasting power. If you've been comparing options, you've probably wondered about vinyl vs. laminate flooring durability. Understanding how each material holds up over time will help you make a smarter investment for your home. This guide breaks down everything you need to know. By the end, you'll feel confident picking the floor that fits your lifestyle. What Does Durability Really Mean for Flooring? When we talk about flooring durability, we're really looking at a few key factors. These include scratch resistance, moisture tolerance, impact strength, and overall lifespan. A durable floor can handle daily foot traffic without showing major wear. It also resists common household hazards like spills, pet claws, and dropped objects. Your home's specific conditions play a big role too. A kitchen floor faces different challenges than a bedroom floor, so durability needs vary from room to room. Before you start shopping, it helps to see how different styles look in your actual space. Floorma flooring visualizer lets you preview both vinyl and laminate options in your own room, so you can focus on durability without guessing about appearance. Understanding these basics gives you a strong foundation. Now, let's look at how each flooring type actually performs. How Durable Is Vinyl Flooring? Vinyl flooring is made from synthetic PVC layers, which makes it naturally flexible and resilient. This composition gives it a unique ability to absorb impact without cracking or chipping. One of vinyl's biggest strengths is its waterproof core. You can install it in bathrooms, kitchens, and basements without worrying about moisture damage. Most modern vinyl planks come with a protective wear layer on top. This layer shields the surface from scratches, scuffs, and everyday foot traffic. Luxury vinyl plank (LVP) takes durability even further. Higher-end options feature thicker wear layers that can withstand heavy use for decades. However, vinyl isn't completely invincible. Sharp objects and heavy furniture can sometimes leave permanent dents if you're not careful with protective pads. Overall, vinyl ranks high on the durability scale. It's especially impressive in wet or high-traffic areas of your home. How Durable Is Laminate Flooring? Laminate flooring uses a layered construction built around a dense fiberboard core. On top sits a photographic image layer covered by a hard, clear resin coating. That resin layer is what gives laminate its excellent scratch resistance. In fact, laminate often outperforms vinyl when it comes to resisting surface scratches from pets or furniture. You'll also find that laminate handles heavy foot traffic remarkably well. It tends to maintain its appearance in busy hallways and living rooms for years. However, laminate has one notable weakness. Its fiberboard core is vulnerable to moisture, which can cause swelling and warping if water seeps between the planks. This makes laminate a poor choice for bathrooms or laundry rooms. Even minor spills should be wiped up quickly to prevent long-term damage. Despite this limitation, laminate remains a strong contender. It offers impressive hardness and wear resistance at a very affordable price point. Vinyl vs. Laminate: A Direct Durability Comparison Now that you understand each material individually, let's put them head to head. When comparing vinyl vs. laminate flooring durability side by side , the differences become much clearer. Vinyl wins decisively in moisture resistance. Laminate wins in scratch and scuff resistance on the surface level. For impact resistance, vinyl's flexible composition absorbs shocks better. Laminate's rigid core can crack under heavy impact, though this is rare during normal use. In terms of fading, both floors perform similarly. Quality options from either category come with UV-resistant coatings that protect against sun damage. Your specific rooms and lifestyle should guide your choice. If you're unsure how each option will look throughout your home, the Floorma laminate floor visualizer can help you compare styles across rooms before committing. Neither flooring type is universally better. The right pick depends entirely on where you're installing and how your household uses the space. Scratch Resistance: Which Floor Wins? Scratch resistance matters a lot, especially if you have pets or kids at home. This is one area where laminate often has a slight edge over vinyl. Laminate's aluminum oxide top layer creates an extremely hard surface. Dog nails, chair legs, and toy wheels are less likely to leave marks on laminate compared to vinyl. Vinyl is softer by nature, which means it's more prone to surface scratches. However, many premium vinyl products now include enhanced wear layers that significantly improve scratch protection. If scratch resistance is your top priority, look for products with higher AC ratings for laminate. For vinyl, a wear layer of 20 mil or thicker will give you the best defense against daily wear and tear. Keep in mind that both floors benefit from simple precautions. Felt pads under furniture and regular sweeping go a long way toward preserving either surface. Moisture and Water Resistance Water resistance is often the deciding factor between these two floors. If your home has moisture-prone areas, this section is especially important for you. Vinyl is 100% waterproof from top to bottom. You can submerge a vinyl plank in water, and it won't swell, warp, or degrade. Laminate, on the other hand, is only water-resistant on the surface. If water gets underneath or between the seams, the fiberboard core absorbs it and expands. Some newer laminate products feature water-resistant cores that perform better than traditional options. Still, even the best water-resistant laminate doesn't match vinyl's complete waterproof capability. For kitchens, bathrooms, mudrooms, and basements, vinyl is the clear winner. Laminate works best in bedrooms, living rooms, and other dry spaces throughout your home. How Long Will Each Floor Last? Lifespan is the ultimate measure of flooring durability, and both options offer solid longevity. Your maintenance habits and installation quality will affect how long either floor actually lasts. Quality vinyl flooring typically lasts between 15 and 25 years. Luxury vinyl products with thicker wear layers can push that number even higher with proper care. Laminate flooring offers a similar range, usually lasting 15 to 25 years as well. High-quality laminate in a dry, well-maintained environment can sometimes exceed 30 years. The key difference is how each floor ages over time. Vinyl tends to develop dents and discoloration, while laminate is more likely to chip or peel at the edges. Regular cleaning and simple preventive measures extend the life of both floors significantly. A little ongoing care can add years of beautiful performance to your investment. Which Flooring Is Right for You? Choosing between vinyl and laminate ultimately comes down to your home's unique needs. Both floors deliver strong value, but they each shine in different situations. Go with vinyl if you need waterproof performance. Bathrooms, kitchens, and basements benefit most from vinyl's complete moisture immunity. Choose laminate if scratch resistance and a natural wood look are your top priorities. Laminate offers a harder surface that stands up well to daily wear in dry areas of your home. When it comes to vinyl vs. laminate flooring durability, there's no single winner for every household. Your lifestyle, your budget, and your room conditions all play a part in the final decision. Before making your choice, take advantage of the Floorma flooring visualizer to see both options in your space. Seeing the floors in your actual room makes the decision feel much easier and more confident. Whatever you choose, you're investing in a floor that can look great for years to come. Just match the material to the room, and you'll enjoy beautiful, long-lasting results.

The integration of energy storage solutions into residential and commercial solar power systems has become an essential consideration for those aiming to maximise energy efficiency and independence. Sigenergy battery systems represent a significant advancement in this field, offering reliable, efficient storage capabilities. Understanding the associated costs, installation process, and typical timeline is crucial for potential users seeking to adopt these innovative solutions. The expertise of Sigenergy installers plays a critical role in ensuring optimal system performance and longevity. Overview of Sigenergy Battery Systems Sigenergy offers state-of-the-art battery systems designed to complement solar power installations. These batteries store excess solar energy generated during daylight hours for use during periods of low sunlight or at night, thus maximising self-consumption and reducing reliance on grid electricity. With advanced lithium-ion technology, Sigenergy batteries deliver high energy density, extended lifecycle, and enhanced safety features. articles.title: Regulatory Debate
articles.author: Tiqua Jackson
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. A gambling company used to be relatively easy to identify. It ran the betting shop, took the money and advertised under its own name. Online, that chain can involve half a dozen businesses before a customer ever reaches the actual operator. Someone might first read a review, follow an affiliate link, see an ad retargeted through social media and then use a payment service that has nothing to do with the site itself. None of those companies necessarily controls the product. They are still involved in getting it in front of people. Sweepstakes gaming has brought that awkward relationship into focus because regulators are no longer looking only at the company running the games. The category itself also takes some explaining. Many sweepstakes platforms use virtual currencies, sometimes with a second currency tied to prize redemption, and availability can change depending on the state. Reviews now spend a fair amount of time explaining those details, as Strafe highlights in their social gaming review series , where the differences between social play, sweepstakes coins and state restrictions are part of the discussion rather than something buried at the bottom of the page. That kind of information matters because the promotion of a product can travel much further than the product itself. The publisher is no longer standing outside the debate New York offers a good example of how wide the regulatory net can become . Its current law covering online sweepstakes games does not stop at operators. It also names payment processors, geolocation providers, platform providers, gaming-content suppliers and media affiliates among the businesses prohibited from supporting covered games in the state. For a media company, that changes the conversation considerably. A publisher can run an article about a service without operating that service, handling a customer's money or having any control over the game. If the article contains an affiliate arrangement, however, the relationship is no longer purely editorial either. This is not a new question. The Federal Trade Commission has long expected affiliate relationships to be disclosed clearly enough that readers understand when a publisher may earn money from a recommendation or link. What is newer is the possibility that a publisher also has to think about whether the underlying product can be promoted in every place where the article might be read. A website may have readers in all fifty states. The service being discussed may not. That mismatch is difficult to solve neatly. Search engines do not stop ranking an article at a state border, and an old review can continue attracting traffic long after the legal position around the product has changed. How far should responsibility travel? There is a reasonable argument behind broader regulation. If a product is restricted but the advertising network, payment system and affiliate traffic continue working exactly as before, the restriction has limited effect. The harder part is deciding how much responsibility belongs to each company in that chain. A payment processor can serve thousands of unrelated businesses. A publisher may cover several industries and have no role in the day-to-day operation of the companies it writes about. An ad platform can distribute campaigns automatically across a large network. They are all involved, but not in the same way. That distinction gets lost when every business surrounding a digital product is discussed as though it performs the same job. Publishers have their own decisions to make here. A review can be useful without being an endorsement, but the difference needs to be visible in the writing. If state availability is limited, saying so is more useful than pretending the internet has no geography. If an affiliate relationship exists, readers should not have to hunt for it. None of that settles the larger legal argument. It does make the media side of it easier to understand. The debate around sweepstakes gaming is likely to keep changing because the states are not all taking the same approach, and the companies involved are not limited to casino operators. What makes the subject interesting is that it exposes something much broader about online commerce: the company selling the product is now only one part of the route that brings people to it. Regulators are trying to work out how far along that route responsibility should extend. Publishers, advertisers and technology providers will have to work out where they stand before the answer becomes clearer.

articles.title: How Cold Weather Affects Electric Dirt Bike Range, Battery Life, and Performance
articles.author: Sejal Desai
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Cold weather can change how an electric dirt bike performs, especially when temperatures drop below freezing. Riders may notice a shorter riding range, slower acceleration, or reduced power when climbing hills. These changes are often related to battery temperature, increased energy demand, and riding conditions rather than a permanent battery problem. For anyone choosing an electric dirt bike for adults, understanding how low temperatures affect battery performance can help set realistic range expectations, prevent avoidable battery wear, and make winter rides more predictable. With the right preparation and maintenance habits, riders can reduce the impact of cold weather on their electric dirt bikes. Why Cold Weather Reduces Electric Dirt Bike Range and Power Cold weather affects electric dirt bikes in several ways. Battery chemistry, power delivery, and the extra energy required to ride on winter terrain can all contribute to a noticeable change in performance. Low Temperatures Reduce Available Battery Energy Lithium-ion batteries operate through chemical reactions that become less efficient at low temperatures. When a battery is cold, its internal resistance increases, making it harder to deliver energy efficiently. As a result, riders may have less usable energy available during a winter ride than they would under moderate conditions. This does not automatically mean the battery has suffered permanent damage. Performance often improves as the battery returns to an appropriate operating temperature. However, repeated exposure to unsuitable temperatures, particularly during charging, can affect battery health over time. Battery Voltage Can Drop Under Heavy Loads Electric dirt bikes draw substantial current during hard acceleration, steep climbs, and demanding off-road sections. In cold conditions, increased battery resistance can cause a greater voltage drop under these loads. Riders may experience weaker acceleration, reduced climbing performance, or a power limitation triggered by the battery management system. These effects can be more noticeable when the battery is already low on charge. A higher peak motor-power rating does not eliminate this issue. Actual performance depends on the battery's temperature, state of charge, current limits, and the bike's overall electrical system. Winter Terrain Requires More Energy Cold temperatures are only part of the problem. Mud, wet ground, loose gravel, snow, and frozen ruts can increase rolling resistance or require more frequent acceleration and corrections. Short daylight hours and strong headwinds may also influence riding conditions. If a route requires more energy per mile than usual, the battery will run down faster even when its underlying condition has not changed. How Much Range Can an Electric Dirt Bike Lose in Cold Weather? There is no universal percentage for winter range loss. The result depends on temperature, battery condition, terrain, rider weight, speed, tire pressure, and how aggressively the bike is ridden. The following table illustrates how a hypothetical 60-mile range would change under different levels of range reduction. These figures are mathematical examples, not measured cold-weather test results or predictions for a particular model. Actual results may fall outside these examples. A mild winter ride on firm ground may cause relatively little change, while a long ride in freezing conditions on soft or uneven terrain may consume substantially more energy. For better trip planning, use your own bike's observed range in similar conditions rather than relying exclusively on the advertised maximum range. Leave a battery reserve for unexpected detours, difficult terrain, and the return journey. How to Maintain Electric Dirt Bike Performance in Winter A few practical habits can help riders manage cold-weather performance and protect the battery from avoidable stress. Before Riding Check the battery charge: Start with enough charge for the planned route and a reasonable reserve. Store the battery appropriately: When the battery is removable, follow the manufacturer's instructions for indoor storage and temperature limits. Inspect the tires: Use the tire pressure recommended for your bike and riding conditions. Do not reduce pressure arbitrarily to compensate for slippery terrain. Plan a shorter route: Allow for uncertain range, especially on unfamiliar trails or in freezing weather. Check the bike: Inspect the brakes, controls, tires, chain or drivetrain, and other components before setting out. During the Ride Use smooth acceleration: Avoid repeated full-throttle starts and unnecessarily aggressive acceleration when traction is limited. Monitor battery status: Watch for unusual voltage drops, power limitations, or rapid changes in the displayed range. Adjust your riding pace: Slower, smoother riding may reduce energy demand and improve control on slippery surfaces. Keep a reserve: Turn back early if the battery is dropping faster than expected. After Riding Keep the battery dry: Wipe away moisture and inspect the battery area and electrical connections according to the manufacturer's maintenance guidance. Let a cold battery warm safely: If the battery has become very cold, allow it to return to the manufacturer's recommended charging temperature before connecting the charger. Follow charging temperature limits: Do not charge a lithium-ion battery below its permitted charging temperature. Some batteries require a specific minimum temperature, so check the owner's manual rather than assuming all models are the same. Store it correctly: Follow the manufacturer's recommendations for charge level, temperature, and storage duration if the bike will not be used for an extended period. These steps cannot eliminate every effect of winter weather, but they can help reduce avoidable energy consumption and support long-term battery care. Is Cold-Weather Power Loss Normal or a Sign of a Problem? Some reduction in range or power is expected in cold weather. However, a sudden or unusually large change should not automatically be attributed to temperature. The following checks can help distinguish ordinary winter performance changes from issues that may need attention. If performance does not improve after the battery returns to a suitable temperature, investigate other causes. Avoid opening the battery pack or attempting electrical repairs unless you are qualified to do so. Choosing an Electric Dirt Bike for Cold-Weather Riding When comparing electric dirt bikes for adults, look beyond advertised top speed and maximum range. Battery capacity, the manufacturer's operating-temperature guidance, braking performance, suspension, tire setup, and the availability of replacement parts can all influence the ownership experience. A larger battery capacity may provide more energy to work with, but it does not guarantee a particular winter range. Likewise, a powerful motor does not prevent cold-related voltage sag. Riders should compare the complete system and consider how the bike will be used. Example: HappyRun G300 Pro The HappyRun G300 Pro is one example of a high-powered model riders may consider when evaluating anadult electric dirt bike for off-road use. Its published specifications include: Peak motor power: 6,500W Battery: 72V 30Ah lithium battery Advertised range: Up to 70 miles Advertised top speed: Up to 50 mph in off-road mode Brakes: Hydraulic brakes Suspension: Full suspension Maximum payload: 350 lbs These are manufacturer-listed specifications, not independent test results. The advertised range should not be treated as a guaranteed winter range, and actual speed and range depend on riding conditions, battery charge, terrain, and other factors. For riders comparing a fastest electric dirt bike or a high-performance off-road model, it is worth separating headline performance figures from the practical requirements of winter riding. A bike's battery system, fit, braking setup, and suitability for the intended terrain matter just as much as its advertised power. Before riding any high-powered electric dirt bike, check the manufacturer's instructions and the local rules governing where the vehicle can be used. A model's off-road speed rating does not automatically make it legal for public roads or shared trails. Prepare for More Reliable Winter Rides Cold-weather range loss is usually the result of several factors working together: reduced battery efficiency, voltage drop under load, and increased energy demand from the terrain. Understanding these factors helps riders plan routes more carefully and recognize when a change in performance may indicate a problem. Keep the battery within its recommended temperature limits, use smooth acceleration, inspect the bike regularly, and leave enough charge for the return journey. Most importantly, treat advertised range as a reference point rather than a guarantee—especially when riding in cold or unpredictable conditions. FAQs Does cold weather permanently damage an electric dirt bike battery? Cold weather does not automatically cause permanent damage, but operating or charging a battery outside its specified temperature limits can affect its performance, safety, and lifespan. Follow the manufacturer's storage, operating, and charging instructions. Should I charge my electric dirt bike battery immediately after a winter ride? Not necessarily. If the battery is below its permitted charging temperature, allow it to warm naturally to the recommended range before charging. Always follow the battery manufacturer's instructions, and never use direct heat to warm a battery. Why does my electric dirt bike lose power when climbing hills in cold weather? Climbing requires more current from the battery. Low temperatures can increase internal resistance and cause a greater voltage drop under load, potentially triggering power limits. A low state of charge or a battery-related issue may make the effect more noticeable. Can an electric dirt bike with a 50 mph top speed reach that speed in winter? Not necessarily. A published top speed is a reference figure under suitable conditions, not a winter performance guarantee. Cold temperatures, battery charge, terrain, traction, rider load, and safety conditions can all affect achievable speed. Riders should never attempt to reach maximum speed on icy or slippery ground.

articles.title: Luxury Yacht Charter
articles.author: Britta Hedlund
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Few holidays combine privacy, comfort, and exploration the way a yacht trip does. You wake up in a different bay each morning, dine with the sea in front of you, and set the pace of every day. A luxury yacht charter lets you reach coves and coastal towns that are difficult to enjoy from land. Planning one takes more than choosing a destination, though. The yacht, the season, the crew, and the fine print all shape the experience. These seven factors will help you make confident decisions before you set sail. 1. Choose a Destination That Matches Your Travel Style Start with the kind of holiday you want. Some travelers picture quiet days anchored in turquoise water, while others want to hop between islands or spend evenings in lively harbor towns. Popular charter regions each offer something different: The Mediterranean combines historic ports, glamorous resorts, and varied coastlines across Italy, France, Spain, and Greece. The Caribbean suits those who want warm water, white-sand beaches, and relaxed island-hopping. The Adriatic, especially along Croatia’s coast, offers medieval towns, national parks, and sheltered anchorages. Think about the scenery, the local attractions, and the activities along your likely route, such as snorkeling, hiking, or exploring local restaurants. The right destination is the one that fits how you like to spend your time. 2. Select the Right Yacht for Your Needs Once you have a destination in mind, consider the vessel itself. When planning a luxury yacht charter , the main types suit different priorities: Motor yachts are faster and offer more interior space, which makes them popular for covering longer distances in comfort. Sailing yachts give a more traditional experience, with a quieter pace and a closer connection to the water. Catamarans have wide decks, stable handling, and shallow drafts that allow access to smaller bays. Beyond the type, look at the number of guests and cabins, the layout of the living areas, and the onboard facilities. A yacht’s size and design affect everything from how private your group feels to how easily you can swim or use water toys. Match the vessel to your group’s needs, not just its looks. I moved the keyword to the intro sentence so it appears only once in this section and reads naturally. If you’d prefer it at the end instead, I can restore the original closing line and remove it from the opening. 3. Set a Realistic Budget Decide what you are comfortable spending before you start browsing. It narrows your options and prevents disappointment later. The base charter price is only part of the cost. Many charters add expenses on top of the quoted fee, including: Fuel Food and beverages Crew gratuities Marina and port fees Ask for a clear breakdown of what the quote covers. A transparent provider will explain what is included and what is not, so you can plan the total cost without surprises. 4. Decide When to Travel Timing affects weather, sea conditions, availability, and price. Research the best seasons for your destination. The Mediterranean is most popular in summer, while the Caribbean has its own peak months and weather patterns to consider. Peak periods offer reliable weather but bring higher prices and fuller harbors. Off-peak periods can mean lower rates and quieter anchorages, though conditions may be less predictable. If you have specific dates or a particular yacht in mind, book early, since the best vessels are often reserved well in advance. 5. Understand the Crew and Onboard Services The crew has a large influence on how your trip feels. Find out whether the yacht comes with a professional captain and crew, and what roles they fill. Ask about the services on offer, such as: Private dining and chef-prepared meals Housekeeping Itinerary assistance Water sports and equipment A skilled, attentive crew will handle the sailing and anticipate your needs so you can relax. Their experience also matters for local knowledge, including quiet anchorages and trusted restaurants. Ask about the crew’s background and how the service is tailored to guests. 6. Plan Your Itinerary, but Leave Room for Flexibility Make a list of the beaches, islands, and coastal towns you would like to visit, then discuss possible routes and travel times with the captain or charter provider. They can tell you what is realistic in the time you have. Resist the urge to fit in too much. A packed schedule turns a relaxing holiday into a race between ports. Leaving some days open also helps with weather, which can change plans at short notice. Some of the best moments come from spontaneous discoveries, like a secluded bay the captain recommends or an unplanned lunch in a village you had not heard of. 7. Check the Booking Terms and What’s Included Before you commit, read the charter agreement carefully. Confirm the key terms: Payment schedule: when deposits and balances are due Cancellation policy: what happens if your plans change Security deposit: how much is held and when it is returned Insurance: what is covered for the vessel, guests, and cancellations Also check which amenities, activities, and services are part of the price. Water toys, specialty meals, and extra services are sometimes charged separately. Clarify any additional costs before you confirm so there are no surprises on board. Final Thoughts Planning a yacht holiday becomes much easier when you work through these seven factors one at a time. Choosing a destination that suits your style, the right vessel, a realistic budget, and sensible timing sets a strong foundation. Understanding the crew, building a flexible itinerary, and reviewing the terms carefully takes care of the rest. The aim is an experience that matches your expectations, travel preferences, and budget. Take your time to research your options, ask questions, and prepare properly. A well-planned luxury yacht charter lets you step aboard knowing the details are handled, so you can enjoy the water.

Best Truck Accident Lawyers in Pearland, TX: 6 Firms to Consider A crash with an 18-wheeler on Highway 288 or the Sam Houston Tollway can turn life upside down in seconds. Medical appointments, insurance calls and missed work pile up fast, and choosing a lawyer can feel like one more burden. Pearland sits just south of Houston, so most of the firms handling serious trucking cases for local residents are based in the city. This shortlist covers six Houston-area firms worth a consultation, what each one emphasizes and the questions that help you compare them. Key Takeaways Our first pick stands out for a clearly published case process, from free consultation and investigation through negotiation and court. Several firms on this list highlight board certification in Personal Injury Trial Law, a specialist credential from the Texas Board of Legal Specialization. Trucking cases depend on evidence such as driver logs and black-box data, so ask each firm how quickly it moves to preserve records. Nearly every firm works on contingency, but the percentage and the handling of case expenses vary, so get both in writing. Texas generally gives you two years from the crash to file a personal injury lawsuit. How We Picked We reviewed each firm's truck accident practice pages, attorney biographies and published fee information in November 2026. We looked for five things: a dedicated commercial-truck practice, a described investigation process, named credentials, practical access for Pearland residents and clear fee terms. 1. The Morgan Legal Group, PLLC This Houston firm maintains a dedicated 18-wheeler accident practice and lays out exactly how it handles a case from the first call to a possible trial. For Pearland residents who want a firm that explains its process up front, The Morgan Legal Group, PLLC is a strong first consultation. Pros A six-stage process covering consultation, investigation, personalized strategy, communication, negotiation and court representation Investigation that includes gathering evidence, reviewing medical records and consulting with experts A stated priority on consistent, transparent communication and regular case updates A 100% free initial consultation Cons The fee percentage is set in the engagement agreement, so confirm it at the consultation The office is in downtown Houston at 440 Louisiana Street, Suite 910, a drive up Highway 288 from Pearland Fees: The firm describes contingency-based fees, meaning attorney fees come from a recovery. Request the percentage and expense terms in writing. Best for: Victims of catastrophic truck crashes who want a firm built around trial preparation. 3. Sutliff & Stout Sutliff & Stout is a Houston injury firm founded by Graham Sutliff and Hank Stout. Both founders are board certified in Personal Injury Trial Law by the Texas Board of Legal Specialization. Pros Two board-certified founding partners A dedicated Houston truck accident practice Describes working with experts and handling insurer communications Free case evaluation and no legal fees without a financial recovery Cons Trucking is one of several practice areas rather than an exclusive focus The office is on Post Oak Boulevard in Uptown Houston, farther from Pearland than downtown Fees: No legal fees without a recovery. Ask separately about case expenses. Best for: Readers who place a high value on specialist trial credentials. 4. Pros Describes collecting driver logbooks, black-box data and electronic control module records Consults treating physicians and medical experts Free consultations and contingency-based fees Statewide representation Cons No individual fee percentage is published Confirm where consultations and meetings would take place Fees: Contingency-based. Ask how expert fees are funded and deducted. Best for: Readers who want a detailed conversation about vehicle and driver records. 5. Abraham Watkins Abraham Watkins is a long-established Houston firm with a downtown office. Its truck accident page describes a rapid-response investigation team. Pros A rapid-response team for early investigation Focus on preserving black-box data, driver logs and scene photographs Board-certified personal injury trial lawyers among its attorneys Contingency-based representation Cons Its stated trucking focus is severe injury and wrongful death, so ask early about less serious claims No individual fee percentage is published Fees: Contingency-based. Terry Bryant Accident & Injury Law Terry Bryant opened his Houston firm in 1985. He is board certified in Personal Injury Trial Law and served 22 years as a municipal judge in Spring Valley Village. Pros A board-certified founder with experience on the bench A dedicated Houston truck accident practice page Free consultation Says the fee percentage is agreed in writing before work begins Cons The office is on the Katy Freeway in west Houston, the longest drive from Pearland on this list Ask which attorney would personally handle your case Fees: Contingency-based, with the percentage agreed in writing up front. Ask separately about expenses. Best for: Readers who value a long-established firm and a founder with judicial experience. Questions to Ask at Every Consultation Rule 1.04(d) of the Texas Disciplinary Rules of Professional Conduct requires contingency fee agreements to be in writing and to state how the fee is determined. Read the expense provisions as closely as the percentage. Bring the same questions to each meeting so the answers are easy to compare: Who will handle my case day to day? Which evidence will you request first, and how fast? Are expenses deducted before or after the attorney fee? What would I owe if there is no recovery? How often will I get updates, and from whom? For a broader look at how claims move from crash to settlement, see this guide to Texas personal injury cases . Conclusion Our first pick is the strongest starting point for Pearland residents who want a firm with a clearly explained process and a commitment to regular communication. Its free consultation makes it easy to learn how the firm would approach your crash before committing. The other five firms each bring something specific, from trial-first preparation and board-certified founders to detailed truck-evidence collection and judicial experience. Consider meeting with more than one, compare written fee terms side by side and move quickly, since trucking evidence can disappear in weeks. This article is general information, not legal advice. Check the proposed lawyer's Texas license and relevant trucking experience before you hire. FAQ How long do I have to file a truck accident lawsuit in Texas? Texas generally allows two years from the date of the crash to file a personal injury lawsuit. Evidence such as driver logs and black-box data can be lost much sooner, so it helps to speak with a lawyer early. How much does a truck accident lawyer cost? Most truck accident lawyers work on contingency, taking a percentage of any recovery. Texas requires that agreement in writing, so compare the percentage and the treatment of expenses before signing. What if I was partly at fault for the crash? Texas uses a modified comparative fault rule. You can recover damages if you are 50% or less responsible, though your award is reduced by your share of fault. Do I need a lawyer based in Pearland? Not necessarily. Many experienced trucking lawyers serving Pearland are based in Houston, so focus on trucking experience, credentials and communication, then confirm how meetings would work. What evidence matters most in an 18-wheeler case? Driver logs, black-box and electronic control module data, maintenance records, scene photos and medical records are often central. articles.title: Economics News for Workers, November 2026
articles.content: A Gallup poll on the eve of the election measured the issues of most salience to American voters. Unsurprisingly, the state of the economy was considered the most important, with 87 percent rating it either extremely or very important. However, a close runner-up was healthcare, which has been all but absent from the national discussion. Other top issues included the war in Iran, income and wealth distribution, and gas prices. Common Dreams has noted that the national movement towards single-payer health insurance, also known as Medicare for All, has been reinvigorated with the midterm elections. Strong new supporters of single payer include Abdul El-Sayed (D-MI) and Troy Jackson (D-ME) in the Senate, along with Claire Valdez, Brad Lander, Darializa Avila Chevalier (D-NY), Dr. Jasmine Clark (D-GA), and Melat Kiros (D-CO) in the House of Representatives. While it is unlikely that a bill will be signed while Trump is in office, stalwart supporters like Bernie Sanders (I-VT) plan to introduce Medicare for All into Congress once again. The New York Times recently covered yet another aspect of the dysfunction of our private insurance system . A 2022 bill, the No Surprises Act, was passed by a wide bipartisan majority to ensure patients wouldn’t be saddled with excessive bills when facing emergencies and being unable to pick their doctors. The Act created an arbitration system which was supposed to resolve the disputes between insurers and providers regarding these medical bills. However, providers responded to the Act by swamping the system with millions of claims, often overinflating by many multiples of the cost of providing emergency care. And increasingly insurers — especially big for-profit insurers Anthem and Cigna — have responded by just ignoring the arbitration results and refusing to pay the medical bills. While patients are still insulated from paying these bills directly, the costs related to the arbitrations and unpaid claims are ultimately borne across the insurance risk pool and hospital systems, driving up overall costs. Meanwhile, The Center for Budget and Policy Priorities has broken down how the negative changes wrought by the Trump Administration have impacted enrollees in Affordable Care Act marketplace health plans during the 2027 open enrollment period. Overall, unsubsidized premiums are set to increase by 15 percent, although compared to last year, enrollees will be insulated from more of the increase, if only because they already experienced a massive premium spike with the end of the extended premium credits in the previous year. In addition, immigrants in the U.S. lawfully who do not hold a green card (including refugees and those granted asylum or humanitarian parole) will no longer have access to premium credits. Share of National Income Going to Workers Sinks A recent study of data collected from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) found the share of U.S. income which went towards worker’s wages was steady at a bit north of 60 percent from the end of World War II until around twenty-five years ago. Since that time, it’s declined by almost ten percent. Even within the share which still remains with workers, analysis by the Economic Policy Institute has found that an increasing proportion are taken up by the top 1 percent, and especially the top 0.1 percent, as “excess” wages which were extracted through lowering living standards for lower-income jobs were sopped up by the executive class. President Trump Makes $2.7 Billion Off the Presidency President Trump has been unique among recent Presidents in the open degree (particularly in his second term) to which he has sought to monetize the Presidency via “memecoins” and other crypto assets. With the recent midterm elections, The Guardian reports the value of many of these companies has collapsed , with the value of Trump Media and World Liberty Financial plunging. However, President Trump still made over $2.7 billion in his first two years in office; including hundreds of millions off of crypto and novelty coins not tied up in stock of these associated businesses. The Hungry Pay for Tax Cuts for the Wealthy The so-called One Big Beautiful Bill Act paid for its massive tax cuts for the wealthy and businesses in part through deep cuts to the Supplemental Assistance Nutrition Program (SNAP, often referred to as Food Stamps). The Guardian reported recently on the impact of this , with the total number of enrolled people dropping by 5 million, or 13 percent. This is largely due to new requirements that disabled people and those with teenage dependents must work at least twenty hours a week or volunteer to receive benefits. In addition, the percent of administrative costs paid by the states increased from fifty to seventy-five percent, adding additional strain on state budgets. This past week, the Trump Administration unveiled yet another plan to drop additional millions of Americans from having access to SNAP food assistance. Overall the top nine largest companies are on track to amass $95 billion in profits for the third quarter of 2026 alone, with Saudi state-owned Aramco increasing its quarterly net income to $30 billion. State-Owned Bank in North Dakota Popular Across Political Spectrum CNBC recently highlighted a strange remaining quirk of an earlier period of socialist uprising: the Bank of North Dakota. Formed in 1918 during a period where former Socialist Party members formed a Socialist-Populist alliance (The Nonpartisan League), which took over the moribund state Republican Party, the bank has resisted privatization calls for over a century. It remains popular in the state across the political spectrum, managing some $11 billion in assets. Although the bank in many ways operates similarly to private banks, elected officials sit in key decision-making positions, and the state uses its financial base towards the common good, from funding infrastructure projects, to disaster relief, to providing young North Dakotans with access to low-interest student loans. Several states, including Massachusetts, New Mexico, and California, are also considering proposals to set up public banks.
